Ele said: Mr. Speaker, this is a very short Bill indeed which is before the Elouse today. The main purpose of the Bill, as has been indicated, is to increase to $60,000 the amount of protection carried or provided by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation on savings deposits with financial institutions in Canada that are so recognized under the provisions of the Act.
As most Eton. Members know, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation is a Crown corporation that was formed in 1967 by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act. The main purpose of the Corporation is to insure, within limits specified, savings deposits placed by the public with member financial institutions. The existence of deposit insurance has given security and stability to the savings deposit market in Canada and has almost completely eliminated the fear of runs against financial institutions.
All banks and all federally incorporated trust companies and mortgage loan companies that accept deposits are members of the corporation by law. Provincially incorporated trust companies and mortgage loan companies accepting deposits may become members on application if the Province of incorporation concurs and if the financial condition of the company is acceptable to the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.
I can give the House some statistics. As of the end of 1982, 132 federally incorporated institutions were members of the Corporation; 65 were banks and 67 were trust companies or loan companies. At the same time, there were 52 provincially incorporated trust companies and loan companies holding membership.
In so far as the finances of the Corporation are concerned, at the end of 1982 the total assets of the corporation amounted to approximately $255 million. Its income for the year amounted to approximately $14 million in the form of premiums and $25 million in the form of interest. The total deposits insured by the Corporation as of April 30, 1982 amounted to $118 billion. The corporation is a tax-paying institution. It is expected to pay approximately $12 million in taxes in respect of the 1982 taxation year.
As far as the administration of the Corporation is concerned, it is governed by a board of directors comprised of a chairman appointed by Order in Council, and, ex officio, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the Deputy Minister of Finance, the Inspector General of Banks and the Superintendent of Insurance.
The three purposes of the legislation, Mr. Speaker, are as follows: first, to increase the maximum limit of insurance on each deposit, as I have indicated, to $60,000 from the present $20,000; second, to increase the borrowing authority of the Corporation, which naturally flows from the first item; third, to reduce possible misunderstanding where member institutions receive funds which are not insured deposits.
In addition, there are a few technical amendments which are not in the same category of importance as the three items which I have just discussed.
Dealing with these items in order, Mr. Speaker, first as regards the limit on the amount of insurance, as I indicated in the House on January 17, 1983 the Bill provides for an increase of insurance to $60,000 to take effect as of that date; that is, the date on which the Government's intention was announced to the House. Since the time the deposit insurance plan was first adopted in 1967, the limit has been fixed at $20,000 per depositor in each institution. All of the deposits which a depositor has with one member institution are grouped together for the purposes of that limit. However, if an individual has a deposit account in his own name and, for example, another jointly with another person, the two deposits are insured separately. Also, a deposit made by a trustee for a beneficiary is insured separately from a deposit made directly by that beneficiary.
RRSP deposits and RHOSP deposits are insured separately from deposits made directly by the owner of the plan. Thus, Mr. Speaker, although the limit has been $20,000 per depositor for some time, it has in fact been possible to obtain insurance for considerably more than that amount, either in one institution or by deposits through various institutions. The $20,000 limit was initially set with the intention of enabling the Corporation to insure the normal demand in term saving deposits of ordinary Canadians with small or moderate means, but without going so far as to be insuring investments as such and as a result interfere with the normal functioning of the financial market.
We believe that the $20,000 limit has served well and has resulted in all but a very small proportion by number of deposits in member institutions being insured, and even by amount, the $20,000 insurance limit covered a substantial portion of all deposits made with all institutions. Current estimates show that the $20,000 limit covered 63 per cent of all deposits in banks and 76 per cent of deposits in trust companies and loan companies.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, the Government recognizes, however, that a number of changes have taken place in the year since the $20,000 limit was established. Deposit levels have risen as a consequence of inflation. The existence of deposit insurance has probably had an effect in increasing this type of savings as compared with other possibilities which a person might opt for, such as investments in bonds or stock. And the existence of tax-deferred plans such as Registered Retirement Savings Plans and Registered Home Ownership Savings Plans, which I have referred to, probably have also stimulated savings of the insured type. As a consequence, it seems desirable to make an increase in the level of deposits insured at this time.
The $60,000 limit proposed was recommended by the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs in its report on the profit situation of chartered banks, published in July, 1982. It is estimated that the $60,000 limit will now cover approximately 78 per cent of deposits in banks and

92 per cent of deposits in trust and loan companies. I recommend, Mr. Speaker, to all Hon. Members the rationale used by the Members of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs in making that recommendation. I would draw to their attention that Hon. Members such as the chairman, Mr. John Evans, for Ottawa Centre and the ViceChairman, Mr. Peterson from Willowdale, together with Members opposite such as the acting critic for finance, Mr. Blenkarn from Mississauga South and Pat Carney, the Hon. speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The Hon. Minister still has time left, but I should remind him that he should refer to Hon. Members by their ridings, not by personal names. The rule applies to everyone.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you for your admonition. I would like to identify other Members on the Committee. For example, the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) and the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) all joined in support of encouraging the Government to adopt the $60,000 limit which is in the Bill before us today. As I said, I invite Hon. Members to take a look at the study that was done by the Committee and the reasoning put forward by the Committee in urging the adoption of the $60,000 limit.
Now, some suggestions have been received that the limit should be set much higher than $60,000. The Government is conscious of these suggestions and also of the fact that in the United States under the Federal Deposit Insurance Plan the amount has been set at $100,000. However, Mr. Speaker, I understand there is a study in the U.S. which indicates that that amount should be reduced and limited. However, we believe that the limit of $60,000 would be appropriate for the Canadian plan at the present time.
It is important to keep in mind the basic purpose of the plan, which is to insure saving deposits rather than to insure investments at a level where the investor could be expected to exercise his own judgment or, for example, to seek professional advice. It is not desirable to interfere in the normal functioning of the financial market by setting deposit insurance guarantees at a level that puts all other types of investment activity at a disadvantage. It is important to note as well that the main volume of premium funds received by the Corporation comes from large, strong institutions, whereas the smaller and less known institutions are probably the beneficiaries of the plan to an extent out of proportion to their relative size. There is to be some reasonable limit to the extent to which the large institutions, for example, have therefore to carry the load or contribute to a pool of this type.
The Bill proposes no change in the premium structure. Under present rules, the annual premium required of each member institution is one thirtieth of 1 per cent of the amount of insured deposits. However, the Corporation has certain limited authority to reduce the premiums below this level if it believes the fund is adequate.
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation
With respect to borrowing power, the Corporation now has the power to borrow up to $500 million from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. Any such borrowing is to meet financial needs to the extent that the Corporation cannot conveniently do so from its own resources. Any such loans would be at a rate of interest appropriate to the circumstances and would be repaid by the Corporation either from realization of its own assets or from revenue produced by future premiums.
It is important, if CDIC is to play its full role as a stabilizing influence in the savings deposit market, that it be of such size and, of course, have resources sufficient to make clear to everyone concerned that it can reasonably fulfil the function which it is intended to play. The borrowing limit of $500 million, set in 1967, which was adequate at that time, is of course no longer adequate. In the context of this fact, and in concert with the proposed increase from $20,000 to $60,000, it seems appropriate to provide the Corporation with access to larger financial resources to meet emergency needs. Therefore, the Bill proposes that the borrowing authority be raised from $500 million to $1.5 billion.
With respect to possible confusion where a member institution accepts money which is not insured, the Bill proposes that all member institutions be required to mark clearly any instrument issued in return for funds where the transaction does not give rise to insured deposit. I made reference to that as being the third major thrust of the legislation before the House. Certain exceptions are specified in the Bill where it is most unlikely that any misunderstandings would occur. This provision is for the purpose of meeting certain problems which experience has shown have arisen in connection with the operation of the Corporation through its mandate.
The request for this legislation has been reinforced by Hon. Members from all Parties and by Canadians in general who have written to Hon. Members, to myself or to the Department. For example, I have in my hand copies of numerous requests that this legislation be addressed quickly by the Government. For example, I have in my hand a letter from the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) dated March 1, wherein the Hon. Member refers to an urgent inquiry from Mrs. Sinclair of Vernon, Ontario. The Hon. Member recites that she and her husband are worried about bad publicity re the trust companies and do not know what to do, but that they do badly need the $20,000 which will be due to them. The Hon. Member concludes:
I have been asked to refer the matter to you for advice and in view of the time frame involved, I would ask for your advice as quickly as possible-
I have in my hand another letter from the same Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton, again with regard to constituents who are concerned about the same matter, and it is dated February 21. The Hon. Member concludes by requesting an urgent response to this matter.
Similarly, I have in my hand the same kind of letter from other Hon. Members. For instance, the Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty) requests a speedy

response to an inquiry from one of his constituents. A similar letter from the Hon. Member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley) requests a response to an inquiry about the status of this legislation on behalf of constituents. The letter is dated March 28, 1983 and the Hon. Member concludes by saying:
I look forward to receiving your comments to guide me in replying to my constituents.
As I say, I have also received letters from individual Canadians who have written. I have in my hand a second letter from the same Hon. Member, the Hon. Member for Don Valley West, indicating the concern of a constituent. This letter, dated March 11, asks for a report on the status of the legislation.
Therefore, I can assure Your Honour that there is a widespread interest as reflected by many Hon. Members who have written to me on behalf of their constituents asking for advice and a report on the intentions of the Government and the status of the legislation in front of us. I have a letter from the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) inquiring about the suggestion of raising the limit to $100,000, which is a suggestion made by one of his constituents. I have a letter from the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) inquiring about the implications of the legislation as far as the RRSP stock certificate is concerned. I merely refer to those letters in order to demonstrate that, in addition to the direct inquiries from Members of all Parties, they reflect the concern of Canadians generally.
Although we have had the opportunity to appear with officials before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, where some questions have been raised with respect to this matter, I have not had full opportunity to discuss the implications of the legislation with Members of the Official Opposition.
I do have a press report today from the Ottawa Citizen which raises an issue which I think I should deal with before I conclude in order to indicate the Government's position and intention in this legislation. This report attributes to the Hon. Member from the Ontario riding of Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) the statement that it is his Party's wish that the Bill be back-dated several years so that investors in such firms as the defunct ReMor Investment Management Corporation can receive more money back.
When addressing the issue of the effective date of the legislation, I indicated in my opening remarks that it is the Government's intention that the legislation be effective as of the announcement of the legislation, which is January 17. Passage of the Bill, hopefully today, would make it effective on January 17. It is not the Government's intention that the legislation should go into the past beyond the date that the Government publicly announced its intention to change the legislation.
With respect to the specific case of ReMor Investment Management Corporation identified by the Member for Simcoe North, I would add as well that I am holding a report dated March 23 from the Ombudsman of the Province of
Ontario in which he addresses issues raised by the Member for Simcoe North concerning the security of investors who had deposits in that corporation.
I should draw to the attention of Hon. Members the conclusion of the Ombudsman report at page 10, which states that there was maladministration in the registration of ReMor. The Ombudsman goes on to indicate what that consisted of. I have read the report very carefully and I would not recommend that the Government consider coverage under CIDC in this situation because I think it is very clear that it was more than simply maladministration by the provincial Ministry of Consumer and Commercial Relations. In my view, it was gross maladministration. It is my conclusion that the responsibility for the difficulties in that case must be met by the administration responsible, which is the Province of Ontario.
In principle, we do not recommend in this Bill that the legislation be back-dated beyond the date of its public announcement. Second, with respect to the request that it be made to apply retroactively to ReMor, we say that clearly on the basis of the report of the Ombudsman, the Province of Ontario should accept total responsibility for any losses over and above the insured amounts that have been covered by CIDC with respect to the depositors in that corporation.
Although the Ombudsman refers to the federal Government in the report, he is very careful to qualify his remarks by saying that he received no evidence, conducted no investigation and it was only on the basis of hearsay that he suggested that the federal Government be involved. Since he is a former jurist, I suspect that he knew that he really did not have the basis for such a recommendation and for that reason recommended that the Province cover any amount that had been suggested might conceivably be covered by the federal Government.
In conclusion, the Bill before us and the Government's request of Members that the amount of coverage be increased to $60,000 has been well received by the public. It is a matter that has been urged upon the Government not only by Members on this side of the House but by Members of the Official Opposition. As well, it is my understanding from the comments made by the financial critic for the New Democratic Party at hearings of the Finance Committee that the NDP would support the legislation.
There may be some arguments that the legislation should be increased to the larger sum of $100,000, as has been suggested in a Private Member's Bill and by some Members in the House, but I hope that I have indicated the basis for the Government's intention to proceed to the $60,000 limit. It is based largely upon the report of the Finance Committee and on the fact that those who urged the $100,000 limit, using the American experience, must now realize that the Americans themselves are moving toward reducing the $100,000 limit under their program in certain circumstances.
Finally, because this is a self insuring plan for which the financial institutions themselves provide the funding by premiums for the program, we believe it would not be wise to

go beyond the date of the intention expressed by the Government to change the amounts and to go retroactively to those institutions to tell them that they must make additional levies for additional premiums, because in the long run that would simply be a charge against the system and finally against depositors and ordinary Canadians.
I join with the House Leader who urges that this legislation receive attention and disposition by the House at the conclusion of today's business.

Would the Minister advise the House whether the effective date of January 17 will enable the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation to cover the losses people may suffer in Greymac and Seaway inasmuch as both of those corporations and their subsidiaries, Greymac Mortgage and Seaway Mortgage, were seized by the Province of Ontario? In other words, they were put into a form of receivership on January 7. Is it not the case, or arguable perhaps, that the people who were depositors with those corporations lost their money effectively on January 7 and, therefore, would not be covered by a January 17 commencement date?

Mr. Speaker, I indicated in my comments that it was as a result in part of some of the problems that were identified by the difficulties with Crown, Seaway and Greymac which gave rise to Government's introduction of the legislation. Specifically as to whether the legislation would cover all potential claimants in those companies, if the Hon. Member would grant me the opportunity, I would like to confirm with counsel that the legislation as passed would cover those cases. That was the Government's intention. I would want to be doubly sure that in fact would be the effect of the legislation. I will get the answer and give it to the Hon. Member when I have it confirmed, hopefully this morning.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Minister for that answer. It would be our understanding that this Bill should certainly cover Greymac and Seaway and any losses that may result in Crown to depositors. If the opinion is to the contrary, can we accept the Government's undertaking to include an amendment to set out specifically that, notwithstanding January 19 being the date of introduction of this Bill, the Government will nonetheless order and direct the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation to cover these losses at least?
While I am on my feet I have one further question for the Minister. He will know that the Ombudsman for Ontario has
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation
made certain claims with respect to ReMor. ReMor, as the Minister will know, was part of the Astra Corporation. He will also know that we have raised on several occasions in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs the maladministration of the federal Department of Insurance, the Department that supervises trust companies. Will the Minister take a look at those questions with respect to ReMor and Astra and the arrangements? Will he look into the fact that a number of persons made deposits in Astra which deposits never reached Astra? Those deposits went directly into ReMor. Will the Minister take a look again at the statements and the investigation of the Ombudsman to see what he can do to make some ex gratia payment to those who suffered losses as a result of Astra being allowed to conduct itself the way it did, despite warnings and evidence that the company should have been closed up ages ago?

Mr. Speaker, with regard to the first question asked by the Hon. Member as to whether we would accept specifically the amendment he proposed, that is based on supposition that I find an answer from the solicitors to say the legislation does not cover these companies now. If the legislation does not cover Greymac, Seaway and Crown, it would be the intention to ensure they were covered, whether in the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member, through some other device or through some other amendment worded in a different way. I will have to take that question under advisement and report to the Hon. Member. I believe we can do that through further discussion of the Bill as it proceeds, but I will look at that immediately.
With regard to the second question, I dealt with that issue in my opening remarks. I mentioned that I had seen reference to the issue by the Hon. Member for Simcoe North. That is why I urge the Hon. Member for Mississauga South to take a look at the actual report of the Ombudsman for Ontario dated March 23, 1983. In the report, the Ombudsman recites that he has investigated certain claims against the Ministry of Consumer and Commercial Relations for the Province of Ontario. In the first ten pages of that report he details the investigation of the charges that his section conducted under the auspices of the Ombudsman Act for the Province of Ontario. As a result, the Ombudsman concluded that in so far as ReMor was concerned there was maladministration. Let me quote his sentence found on page 10 of his report:
-there was maladministration in the registration of ReMor-
By and large, the two reasons were that the registration should not have been on the basis of information the Ministry had. The Ombudsman concludes ReMor ought not to have been registered. Second, the reasons given for the registration at the time were dependent upon a follow-up monitoring by the same Ministry which, as well, was not conducted. For those two reasons, the Ombudsman found, as he says in his report, "maladministration on the Province's part".
Having read the report, with the greatest respect I would say that it was more than simple maladministration; I would

April 12, 1983
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation
say it was gross maladministration. Those two things ought not to have occurred. Therefore, when you come to the part of the report where the Ombudsman makes certain recommendations flowing from his findings, you find a very curious thing, Mr. Speaker. Dealing with the federal Government, the Ombudsman says:
Without necessarily adopting the following-
Therefore, he disclaims what he has to say following this, which reads:
-I note that federal participation in any compensation scheme has been advocated-
In dealing with the federal role, which is the issue raised with Astra firm which was federally incorporated, and the relationship with ReMor, the Ombudsman is very careful to qualify his remarks and does not adopt them to begin with. Second, he indicates that his remarks are based on hearsay evidence. The hearsay evidence is listed in four paragraphs found on page 11 of his report under items (a), (b), (c) and
(d). In my view, had the Ombudsman the opportunity of talking to federal officials or of investigating the hearsay evidence put to him, he would have found that federal officials disputed the allegations in those sub-paragraphs. Indeed, the federal department successfully disputed those allegations in the Federal Court last year was successful at trial in disputing them. The case is presently under appeal.
It is the position of the federal Government that there is nothing in the Ombudsman's report that advances the case for additional consideration. There is nothing new which the Department has not considered and there is nothing new that the Department has not advanced in a court of law in defence of those allegations. Those matters are still pending.
Having said that, I qualify my comments by indicating to the Hon. Member for Mississauga South that there is the issue of tracing. If that is what the Hon. Member has hit upon, I confirm that the Department is still working with the firm of accountants investigating the relationship of ReMor and Astra. Officials are looking at the issue of the flow through of funds from ReMor to Astra. Solicitors for the federal Department have indicated that legally there could be a basis for a claim in law. Our difficulty is not with the law or the basis of liability; our difficulty thus far has been getting the evidence to substantiate in detail that flow through.
I met with the provincial Minister, Dr. Elgie, in November or December. I requested that kind of evidence or documentation. I have to date received no more information. Obviously the matter has been raised in the Ombsbudman report. Our officials have again gone back to the law firm and the firm of chartered accountants which are investigating. If a proper case for tracing is established, the Department has always indicated that that is a proper basis for a claim and will be entertained by the Deposit Insurance Corporation.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister will know that over the last three years a number of problems were raised in the Committee with respect to the Department of Insurance.
On the insurance side, we have had the defalcation of Cardinal, Strathcona and Pitts. On the trust side we have had Astra Trust, Greymac Mortgage and Seaway Mortgage Corporation. The feeling has developed over a period of time that there is something wrong with the way the Government has been supervising these companies and the way the Department of Insurance has been operating.
Second, the previous Minister introduced a draft Bill together with a suggestion for a new Trust Companies Act. Has the Minister yet had an opportunity to confer with his colleagues on the basis of forming a special committee of Parliament to look into the whole question of the supervision of loan and trust companies and what should be done with respect to changes to the Loan Companies and Trust Companies Act?
The Minister will appreciate that the same propositions are now before the Government of Ontario. Representations have been made to him by the Canadian Bankers Association and the Trust Companies Association of Canada. The Trust Companies Act has been in need of revision for some considerable period of time. There have been promises to introduce a Bill in this regard. At this stage, before going ahead madly with legislation, it might be appropriate for the Government to take the advice of Parliament and have a committee look into the entire question. Has the Minister had an opportunity to this point to discuss such a matter with his colleagues?

Mr. Speaker, I have not discussed the matter in the context of a formal submission to my colleagues in Cabinet. However, I did discuss the matter with the former Minister who had responsibility for this portfolio and who was responsible for issuing the paper calling for public input into the matter.
The Hon. Member for Mississauga South is correct. The Government asked for recommendations from all Canadians. We put a time limit on the public input to that process. I believe we asked for submissions as of the end of November, 1982. We received dozens of comments from interested persons. Some of those comments were late in coming. They were received toward the end of December or early January.
I have not, in consultation with my officials, satisfied myself as to the best method of bringing this matter to a conclusion. For example we have not decided whether there is a need for the matter to be addressed before a committee and whether further public input should be sought. As the Hon. Member says, the matter is now complicated by the unfortunate experience with three provincially incorporated and supervised trust companies in the Province of Ontario, Seaway, Greymac and Crown. By parallel, the mortgage companies which are subsidiaries of those companies were brought into the control of the federal Superintendent of Insurance under the federal Loans Act.
The matter is further complicated in that under the federal legislation a hearing is required when the federal Superintendent moves to take control. A hearing is required for the companies that are sought to be controlled. In those hearings they are permitted to make submissions on the Government's intended
April 12, 1983

action. Those hearings are presently continuing. I spent two full days last week receiving submissions by solicitors and officers of those companies. They were making representations with respect to the federal Government's action to take control of the companies.
I cannot say to the Hon. Member at this time that I have concluded that the best way to have the matter resolved is by reference to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs or whether it should be some other way. I have concluded that I should not make up my mind and I should not proceed to the next step until such time as I have had the opportunity of discussing this matter with the provincial Minister of Consumer and Commercial Relations, Dr. Elgie, and the other provincial Ministers who have similar responsibilities.
The Deputy Ministers of the provincial Ministers of consumer and corporate affairs met last Friday. That meeting was attended by Mr. Hammond, the Superintendent for the federal Department. The issues of sorting jurisdiction and attempting to overcome some of the difficulties that may be experienced because of split jurisdiction were dealt with at the meeting of the Deputy Ministers. As of today I have not received formal advice as to the conclusion of the Deputy Ministers.
I guess I have given the long answer. The short answer would be that I am considering the request of the Hon. Member, but it is premature. I am really not at the point to make the kind of decision that he has invited me to make.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me as a Member of Parliament that any new legislation will have to come before Parliament and that legislation might be expedited if the thoughts of Members were expressed in a committee hearing prior to the legislation being introduced. The Minister will appreciate that today the question of the $60,000 insurance limit can be dealt with rather expeditiously because a committee of this House recommended $60,000. It is rather difficult for the House to say that it will not accept the Finance Committee's recommendation made only a few months ago. It is on that basis that I make the suggestion to the Minister.
While the Minister has certain problems with respect to the management of trust companies under the existing legislation, under the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation legislation rather draconian steps can be taken against both federal and provincial institutions and presumably, under Sections 24 and 25, without hearings. In other words, it is a matter of a report to the Minister and the Minister makes a decision. There is no requirement for public hearings or discussions. The Minister can move quite quickly.
On that basis, why did the Minister not take action against Seaway and Greymac under the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation authority rather than under the loan and trust companies authority vis-a-vis the two mortgage corporations?

Mr. Speaker, there are two reasons why I did not move under the CIDC legislation as opposed to the action now under way under the Loan Companies Act. First, the Department of Insurance of the Government of Canada acts as
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation
the regulatory and inspection agent for the CIDC in all Provinces of Canada with the exception of the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Had the difficulty arisen in any Province except Ontario and Quebec, where the actual regulation and daily, monthly or yearly control is by CDIC, it is conceivable that, having a hands on control relationship with the companies, I might have exercised jurisdiction under that legislation.
In the cases that the Hon. Member has cited in the Province of Ontario, I did not exercise jurisdiction because the Province of Ontario, through its Ministry of Consumer and Commercial Relations, and the companies that were primarily affected, the major players-no pun intended-Crown, Seaway and Greymac Trust, were the big brothers or big sisters, if you want, in the piece. The major action was in those companies.
The mortgage companies, which were federally incorporated and under the supervision of the federal Department, were really subsidiaries and under the control of the management of the provincially incorporated and controlled companies. Hence, the Department, although it shared parallel concerns with the Province, really was a minor player in the larger picture. Obviously the control decisions were made by the interlocking boards of directors and the major decisions were made in the parent company. The mortgage companies subject to federal jurisdiction were really minor players in the piece and that is why, for example, the Province moved first to exercise control in respect of Crown, Seaway and Greymac Trust. The federal Government moved subsequently, but in concert because of parallel concerns and because the companies were all interrelated in directorship, in operations and in investment opportunities. So that in effect, if the complaint of the provincial Government at the operation of the parent companies was one that could be satisfactorily concluded, that in turn would solve the problems with the subsidiary mortgage companies.

Mr. Speaker, I hate to keep on going at this. I wanted to go on with my remarks, but the Minister has raised an issue. The Minister will note that there is a Quebec Deposit Insurance Corporation that handles Quebec companies, but it was my understanding, confirmed by the Minister, that all Ontario companies are registered under the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, as are most other trust companies and desposit taking institutions in the rest of the country. It is only in Quebec where they have their own insurance.
Why, then, as the Minister seems to have indicated today, did the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation delegate its supervisory responsibilities to the Minister of Consumer and Commercial Relations in the Province of Ontario, particularly when it is the credit of Canada, not the credit of Ontario, that is responsible to ante up the losses?

The short answer, Mr. Speaker, is because the Province of Ontario requested it. Second, it is not accurate to say that the delegation was a complete delegation. The Province reports the results of its inspections and supervisory

control to the federal Department of Insurance through the Superintendent of Insurance and his officials, so that they are in constant communication. It is a shared supervisory capacity.

Mr. Speaker, on that basis would the Government give us the undertaking now to terminate that shared responsibility and take responsibility as required under the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation? If Ontario wants to insure its depositors in Ontario registered corporations, let them do so; but if they are going to be insured by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, surely we cannot have a situation where the Government of Canada can slither around and say: "Well, we really are not responsible because we sort of shared the responsibility with Ontario, yet at the same time we are responsible".
Will the Minister now give us an undertaking that this whole business of letting some other Ministry in some other jurisdiction do the supervisory work, presumably on contract or something like that, will cease, that we will do the supervisory work if we are responsible for the losses?

Mr. Speaker, when I made reference to a meeting of the Deputy Ministers of consumer and corporate affairs of the Provinces and the Superintendent of Insurance for the federal Government on Friday of last week, this was presumably one of the issues that was discussed and considered by the officials. But it is a working relationship between the Province of Ontario and the Government of Canada at this time. I have not received the report as to what the conclusions of the meeting of the officials were. It is obviously something that the Ministers for the Province of Ontario and the Province of Quebec will have to consider. As the Hon. It is premature for me to give the undertaking that the Hon. Member has asked for, though it is a matter that is being considered. The timing is quite appropriate because the Province of Ontario, I understand, will be publishing a white paper and asking for public input. dealt with the question of supervision of these companies. I should like to read into the record a question that I put on that occasion and an answer given by Mr. Humphrys, then the Superintendent of Insurance. At page 53:9 of the proceedings of the Finance Committee I stated:
Now the Loan and Trust Companies Act allows a trust company to lend up to 75 per cent of the value of a piece of real estate, a home, for example. What are you doing to monitor that situation to make sure that the companies are not just fuelling the inflationary rise in prices and are not getting themselves in a box so that if the bubble bursts on some of these inflationary prices-prices, I might point out, of properties being sold at very much more than the cost of production-we will not wind up with the situation that existed after 1974 when the bubble burst in the last inflationary boom?
Mr. Humphrys replied:
Mr. Chairman, the comment is correct that the law puts a limit of 75 per cent of the value of the property on the amount of the mortgage loan. That is the limit of our statutory authority to control the mortgage lending of the companies. We attempt to see to it that the values that are put forward to justify compliance with this limit are well considered; but, if the market goes up and the properties are trading at the values, there is nothing that we can do other than exercise such persuasive influence as we have on company management to have regard for the fact that the prices may be pushed up in a temporary inflationary surge and that they should not get themselves hung up too severely on these values.
In other words, the Superintendent of Insurance said that he really did not do anything. I pressed him further with respect to Astra Trust when I said:
To a large extent the answer by some of the people in the Astra Trust case is going to be that all they were doing was lending in relation to the price of the property.
That, of course, was their answer. Then I went on to say:
Are you doing spot checks with these companies, checking out the physicals of what they claim to be mortgages on account on a frequent basis? What checks are you doing?
And later I asked:
All right. Are your people going out and checking those appraisers?
Mr. Humphrys replied:
Not usually, sir, no. If he is a professional and qualified appraiser, we would accept that.
That is exactly what happened to us. The real issue before the people of Ontario at the moment is the purchase of Cadillac properties for $270 million, the subsequent sale of those properties, within days, for $500 million and the mortgaging of those properties to 75 per cent of value based not on $270 million but on $500 million. The whole issue is that the Loan and Trust Companies Act allows companies to make advances on real estate to 75 per cent of value. But what is value, Mr. Speaker? It is in the eye of the beholder. We are involved in guaranteeing deposits of people who put their money in what they think are trust companies, in what they think are secure, guaranteed corporations that are supposed to look after their money as a trustee would, but we know there are some high flyers who are not supervised and who get in the marketplace and take accounts and make loans that are totally inappropriate. They pretend they are staying within the law by pretending that they are using appraised values.
We are going to pass this Bill because we need to, but that does not solve the problem. How many times are we going to allow the situation that existed with Astra, and that now exists
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation
with the Seaway, Crown and Greymac companies, to happen again?
Deposit insurance came into force in this country after the problems that occurred with respect to a corporation called British Mortgage and Trust Company in Stratford. It was a well respected trust company in the Province of Ontario that was taken over by some people who had a little different idea from most of us of what a trust obligation was. They proceeded to do the same thing-to make fancy loans based on imaginary appraisals. The company went under and was bailed out by Victoria and Grey Trust Company. There were no depositor losses at that time but deposit insurance was brought in. Now we have a series of claims and there may be more. As we all know in our own communities, instead of real estate prices rising, in many cases they have tumbled by 15, 20, 25 or 30 per cent. When the properties are mortgaged to the hilt, a tumbling of values creates a situation very rapidly where a property is mortgaged for more than 100 per cent of its value. Yet there seems to be no arrangement by the Department of Insurance, or by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, to force companies to take out of current, proper trust assets mortgages which are in excess of 75 per cent of the value of the property. There seems to be no arrangement by the Department of Insurance properly to appraise and spot check the kinds of investments held which are supposed to be back there to protect depositors.
Let us take a look at some of the evidence given before the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs by Mr. Hammond, the current Superintendent, with respect to the Greymac and Seaway matters. I believe it is important that we go over that evidence today which was presented to the Finance Committee. First of all with respect to the Seaway Mortgage Corporation, the Department of Insurance determined on its own, prior to March 31, 1982, which is over a year ago now, that Seaway was in trouble. It put a $70 million limit on the borrowing of Seaway. It renewed the right of Seaway to do business on a month to month basis. Then all of a sudden this company was not being handled correctly, as is now evident. People who had put money up for guaranteed investment certificates in that company had not even received their guaranteed investment cetificate paper. The accounting records were in abominable shape. And it is now evident that, despite the order that they could not increase their borrowing beyond $70 million, in January they were at $106 million.
I ask you, sir, where is the supervision? How come that corporation was allowed to have people in charge who paid no attention to this Minister, to any Minister, to any Superintendent of Insurance, or to any rules and regulations in connection with the management of trust affairs? The answer is that the policemen either did not have the competency, did not have the staff or did not have the power. I say they had the power, perhaps not the competence. They did not have the intestinal fortitude to blow the whistle and terminate these companies.

The same thing happened with Greymac. Greymac was on a short leash from March 31 onwards, yet people put their savings in Greymac and this Department did not do anything about it. Greymac's associated company, Greymac Credit, was able to go into the open market and buy up the shares of the Crown Trust Company. Yet the Department of Insurance and the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation-managed, I might add, by the same people as the Department of Insurance, the same policemen-did not do anything about it.
The original proprietor of Greymac, Mr. Rosenberg, was able to work with his new proprietor, Mr. Player, and they were able to use the treasury of Crown Trust, the treasury of Greymac, their mortgage corporations and their trust companies, and the depositors' money which was insured by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, to play games and to make maybe $125 million for themselves. If the Department of Insurance and the people supervising the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation had done their duty to Canada, had taken their responsibilities in the way they should have, the damage that was done, and has been done to all sorts of people in the country, would not have occurred. The damage which has been done to the confidence of people in trust and savings organizations, and the damage done to the confidence of investors, would not have happened.
This is a serious matter. We cannot, as a Parliament, allow the kind of poor, inept, incompetent supervision which took place with respect to Greymac, Seaway, Crown and Astra to continue. The people involved in that supervision have an obligation to find other employment. The Government responsible is this Government opposite, because this situation was brought to its attention in the Finance Committee in April, 1981. It was brought to its attention again in December, 1981. I personally asked the former Minister what he was doing with respect to flash audits. He said he was doing nothing. I personally asked him how come the same problem of lack of supervision caused losses in the insurance companies of Caledonia, Strathcona and Pitt? What did he do about it? What is he doing about the trust companies? Why is there not supervision? But nothing was done. Now depositors across Canada are going to wind up paying directly or indirectly larger premiums to the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation to cover losses which should not have occurred, and would not have occurred had there been proper supervision.
We have a palliative. We are going to increase that insurance to $60,000 and we are, presumably, going to bail out the depositors in Greymac, Seaway and Crown. We should be bailing out the depositors in Astra also because, despite what the Minister says, despite the warnings, they did not do anything to clean up their act; and it was because they did not do anything to clean up their act that the Greymac, Seaway and Crown affair occurred. The Minister is still depending on the same people. He still has a meeting of people in Ontario. He still has not changed his method of supervision.
I asked him today why he does not bring Parliament into the picture. Let us have some hearings and get this matter straightened around. All he wants to do is talk about it. But
that is not good enough. This Bill must pass, but that is not good enough, because it will not restore confidence other than the confidence of people who will say: "At least they will cover me for $60,000". What about the $3 million lost by the Peel Board of Education on a deposit made in Greymac effective January 1, 1983?

There are two or three concerns about this Bill. First of all, the limit of $60,000 is an important one. It was suggested by the Committee as being appropriate for ordinary deposits, that type of thing. Unfortunately the Committee did not put its mind to the concern with respect to cumulative registered Canada savings plans. Members will appreciate that if interest is calculated monthly at 12 per cent, money will double itself every five years. So a modest deposit of $5,000 today in a trust company, on that basis, will be worth $10,000 in five years, $20,000 in ten years, and $40,000 in 15 years. In 20 years you are out of luck because it becomes $80,000 and the insurance is only $60,000.
Because Registered Retirement Savings Plans are of such a nature that the tax implication of withdrawing the funds is pretty damaging and they cannot be easily moved around by virtue of the Income Tax Act, it is my feeling that the Government ought to consider some provision-perhaps not now because I think it is urgent that the Bill go through-to protect Registered Retirement Savings Plans to a larger amount than the present limit, and to treat them differently when held by a trust company.
April 12, 1983

The Minister made mention of tax. The Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation pays regular income tax. I suppose this is a method by which Government collects its money. It strikes me that the Government is really insuring the financial system, and why the Corporation should be a profit-making institution is beyond me. It seems to me that it should be a co-operative system that would insure deposits and handle various deposittaking institutions in accordance with the risk presented by those deposit institutions. To make a few dollars, or $12 million as the Minister said, in corporate tax is not, in my view, the important function of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. The Minister might well reflect on the fact that what we really want is deposit insurance.
I think we are not really today addressing this particular concern by trying to figure out how to derive another $1 million or so revenue for the Government of Canada. Surely to goodness deposit insurance is not a method of trying to get a few more dollars of revenue for Canada; it is to make sure that those who deposit funds with our financial institutions have a sense of security.
The Minister mentioned briefly that premiums were going up. It is unfortunate that premiums will have to rise. They have not been one-thirtieth of 1 per cent of the amounts deposited; the arrangement up until now has been one of significant reductions in premiums. So that while the Act calls for a premium of one-thirtieth of 1 per cent on deposit, that has not been the practice. Companies who have paid for a five-year period are only paying additional premiums on additional business coming in. Sir, in fact the premiums are going up because of the defalcations, because of this mismanagement. I call on this Government, as I did earlier, to form a special committee of this House immediately to inquire into loan and trust company legislation and into the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation activities, so that we can have confidence as Members of Parliament that things are being changed, that they are going to be managed directly from now on and that we can say to our constituents, all of us, that they can have faith in the deposit institutions of Canada once again.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak for a very short time on Bill C-142, an Act to amend the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. The New Democratic Party agrees that this Act needs to be passed without delay. We recognize the need for an increase in the insurance levels to protect those people who trust the system and who really in many cases do not know that much about it.
I was a little surprised to find myself agreeing on financial structures with the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). That is not a usual area of agreement as far as our Parties are concerned, but controls over financial institutions need to be increased, to the extent that security of deposits is something which people can continue to count on. There should be controls to the extent that a situation such as the Crown, Greymac and Seaway Trust affair could not happen.
It is very important that we recognize the needs of the innocent depositor who puts money into a trust company, because he is going to need the money some time down the road. It perhaps pays a little better interest, but they are not in there to make a great deal of money. These depositors are not
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation
speculators, they put money in there to save because they are going to use it for their retirement. Those kinds of depositors need to be protected. They are not putting money in because they want to make a great deal of money; they want it to be safe. So we need to look at the financial structure in order to safeguard these depositors. In fact, we should look at the financial structure which allows speculation, because speculation is an attempt by people to make money from nothing. That is not part of the structure of our country.
I believe there is little doubt in many people's minds that inflation is the direct result of high interest rates, exorbitant profits and financial manipulation which makes money from nothing, from speculation. In situations where there is no production of goods, where there is no service rendered, and in our financial structure which we have developed and with which we live, should we allow the kind of money making which does not take into consideration the requirement of protection of the small depositor? Many years ago Christ chased the usurers from the temple. Here in Canada and in most of the capitalistic western countries, we have allowed many of them to come back in a kind of structure which protects very few of the people who are unable to protect themselves.
As long as we are in the kind of system which does lack control, then we as a Parliament, as a Government, must protect those people. Apparently, a great number of institutions do not believe that they have any responsibility toward their clients but, rather, believe they should have as much leeway as possible to make as much money as quickly as possible, without concern for their responsibility toward their clients. Therefore, some kind of protection is needed and should be at such a level that the small investor feels secure in putting his money into a financial institution.
A couple of years ago, the $60,000 limit seemed adequate, and it may, in some ways, still be adequate. However, it may not be adequate two or three years down the way. That is why several Hon. Members of this caucus have suggested that perhaps, while we are changing the limit, we should put it at a higher level, rather than coming back a year or two years from now trying to raise it. We must recognize that if we did put it at a higher level, we would not reduce the effectiveness of the Bill. In fact, we would expand its effectiveness to some extent.
The New Democratic Party will support the quick passage of Bill C-142 because it needs to be passed to protect the small depositors from putting the last parts of their life savings into these companies. It does not mean that our Party is happy with the system, but we do support the quick passage of the Bill, so that the people who do trust the system and make use of it can go on trusting it and using it.

Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis). That was his comment. So our House Leader, in reply, told him to go and see the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) and request that he put it on the Order Paper for debate and that we would pass it. The Minister of State for Finance did not say that he wanted the Bill passed. He did not say that the Government had a sense of urgency that the Bill should be passed. Rather, he said: "Your friends in Toronto want this Bill passed". In other words, he-

speechtext: Your rich Tory friends.

speakerposition: Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party

-has no concern, as far as I am concerned, for the trust industry, the depositors or the trust companies. He is interested only in trying to play little-minded political games. That is the way he has throughout his period of responsibility for the two portfolios we have seen him holding in this House. His purpose was to try to have the Bill passed with no debate. That was his objective. It was a typical Liberal trick. He knows that the federal Government was negligent in the matter involving Astra Trust, so he does not want the matter before the House. He does not want debate. He does not want anything out in the open; he wants to keep it under a cloud. That was his purpose in doing that.
Several of my constituents lost several millions of dollars in the bankruptcy of Astra Trust. The typical, unsophisticated investor went into the Astra Trust offices in Burlington and elsewhere and, in good faith, invested their money. They received a receipt from Astra Trust. This one happens to read: "Mrs. W. Stevens, SI0,000".
When one considers the profile of the average investor in Astra Trust, this is what one finds: a relatively unsophisticated investor. By that, I mean one with no experience in investing at any time in his or her personal history. Perhaps a family that had grown up and a couple was in possession of a house which they were able to sell and from which they made a profit. So mama and papa took the money and split it down the middle, perhaps $40,000 or $50,000, went to Astra Trust and invested it. They thought they were investing in a guaranteed income certificate, guaranteed by CDIC. They found out, to their sorrow, that they had invested in a piece of mortgage, because several weeks later they received a document which stated that they were a partial holder of a mortgage somewhere down in the Niagara Peninsula.
The Minister himself, in his announcement on January 17, has continued his confusing ways. He announced that the Bill was to be introduced and that it would raise insurance limit
from $20,000 to $60,000. So what happened in the trust industry? All the trust companies put advertising up on their walls and advised their clients that the limit was now $60,000. It became so blatant that on March 31 the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation issued a telegram to all CDIC members telling them to stop advising people that the CDIC limit was $60,000. That was a direct result of the Minister's release and the fact that he did not have the muscle in Cabinet to have the matter brought forward. Certainly, it would have been brought forward and debated in short order in the House, but he wanted to cover it up. He did not have the muscle with the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) to get this done. He has confused this matter as did his predecessor.
The liquidation of Astra Trust, the bankruptcy of ReMor Investment Management Corporation and the receivership of C & M Financial Consultants are three events which are interconnected through a common ownership of share stock, common directors, and twisted, crooked business dealings designed at the outset to bilk innocent victims of their life savings.
A committee for the Government of Ontario sat for weeks studying the whole matter. The evidence of the connection between Astra Trust and ReMor is so plain that the only person in Canada who cannot see it is the Minister of State for Finance. He had the audacity to say, as reported in The Globe and Mail of April 8, 1983:
Mr. Cosgrove said he has told Dr. Elgie in the past that he would like to see any evidence of a financial link between Re-Mor and Astra. Such a link would be the "only legal basis on which the federal government could be involved" in any plan to compensate those who have suffered losses.
The link is there and it is very direct. Not only are the depositors of Astra Trust victims, but some of the shareholders have been gutted by a group of financial sharks who left behind a trail of shattered lives, broken dreams, threats of suicide out of despair and a cynicism so deep that it could lead to violence. I have heard many who have come to my office threatening violence.
Victims of the ReMor scam were baited by smooth-talking trust officers who took their money, gave Astra Trust receipts to the victims and switched the money to worthless ReMor mortages. When the victims complained, they were told they were the holders of good, solid First mortgages when, in reality, they owned a piece of a fourth or fifth mortgage on a piece of property that was next to worthless and much of which was under water.
The purists in business practice cannot invoke caveat emptor, "let the buyer beware", because most of the innocent victims who entered the doors of the trust company say on the doors, the walls, the windows and counters the display of advice that Astra Trust was a member of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. They had that warm, comfortable feeling that the Government was there to protect them. Adding to that mixture of deception, the words "guarantee" and "guaranteed" were prominently displayed in the office and in
April 12, 1983

the advertising on the wall charts and brochures. When one adds the fact that Astra Trust was, of course, paying a slightly higher interest rate than other trust companies, one begins to see the dimension of the scam. It was trust company with protection by the Government and it was all guaranteed.
As in most deceptive dealings, there was another side that was not up front or displayed. It was the fact that the trust officers of Astra Trust were also commission agents for ReMor. They were paid a salary by Astra Trust and a commission by ReMor. They took the money from their mark in the trust, Government protected guarantee atmosphere and switched the money into a worthless ReMor mortgage.
The Minister of State for Finance has tried to weasel out of this dirty, smelly, disgusting mess by saying that ReMor is a provincial responsibility. That has been his comment. There are dozens of unanswered questions that must be investigated. Let me list a few. Is the Department of Insurance adequately staffed? Does it have the mandate to perform adequate inspections of the trust industry? After all, it was only a short time ago that Argosy Trust left behind a trail of shattered certificate holders.
How closely were the affairs of Astra Trust monitored by the Department of Insurance? What liaison is there between the federal and provincial Governments? I suspect there is very little.
What leverage does the Department of Insurance have that it can get the Ontario Securities Commission to hold back on a stop trading order on a trust company that has violated the regulations under which it operates? Did the inspectors from the Department of Insurance refer the advertising of Astra Trust to the Ministry of Consumer and Corporate Affairs when it was obvious to anyone that it was misleading? Why did the Department of Insurance not intervene when it was apparent that the trust officers at Astra Trust were acting as commission agents for ReMor? Surely they knew the amount of money that was passing through Astra Trust. If the Government instructed Astra Trust to close down C & M Financial Services when the trust licence was given to Astra Trust, why did it act blindly to the activities of ReMor? Was C & M really closed down? The evidence is to the contrary.
Did the Department of Insurance inspectors' report to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs indicate that bait and switch tactics were being used by Astra Trust officers? If not, why not? They certainly had enough evidence.
What liaison existed between the Department of Insurance and CMHC? That is an interesting question. The present Minister of State for Finance was formerly the Minister of Public Works responsible for housing. A question was put on the Order Paper by my colleague from Simcoe North. He asked if Astra Trust Company was an approved lender for the purposes of purchasing, making and administering approved loans under Part I of the National Housing Act and, if so, what date was such a designation approved, who approved the designation and on what basis; and, if not, had the company ever been so designated and, if so, on what date was such a
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation
designation approved, who approved the designation, and on what basis? This was the reply by the Minister of Public Works who is now the Minister of State for Finance:
I am advised by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation as follows:
Astra Trust was designated an approved lender by an Order in Council November 22, 1979. CMHC reviewed all pertinent information and documentation submitted by the applicant and was satisfied that this applicant met all criteria established by the corporation. On this basis CMHC sought an order in council designating this company as an approved lender.
I suggest that if this was put in chronological order, it would be seen that other investigations were under way at that time. There was no co-ordination at all between the Departments.
How much money was diverted from Astra Trust into a condominium in Spain? Do we really know if the money went to that development, or is it in a numbered account in Switzerland or Liechtenstein? We know that RCMP officials traced the money as far as they could. But were directors of Astra Trust so inept that they would invest trust funds in a venture that was so questionable and which was against their charter, an agreement with the federal Government? Was it chosen, rather, as a front to deliver money to a hidden account so that it could be retrieved at a later date? I suspect that this is what happened.
With a mass of regulatory violations outstanding against Astra Trust after 12 months of operation, why was firm action not taken at that time before the whole mess festered and grew into the tangled fraud that we have before us today?
I could go on, but in the final analysis the bankruptcy of ReMor and the liquidation of Astra Trust is a scar on the entire trust industry. While some in the industry express their views verbally regarding the licensing of Astra Trust, no one in that industry put their concerns in writing, through their trade association, about the licensing of Astra Trust to the Canadian Deposit Insurance Corporation. They knew because they talked privately about Astra Trust and the people who were directing it.
We must ask, whom do you trust? To whom do unsophisticated investors turn when they wish to invest the proceeds of the sale of their home, bequests or other funds that they may have available?
I have contended for some time that we must have an open judicial inquiry, a joint federal-provincial royal commission, if necessary, into this matter. The personal assets of the officers and directors of Astra Trust, ReMor and C & M should be frozen by the Government. The assets of their wives should be frozen so that the inquiry can determine if loans and other funds have been diverted or transferred to second or third persons to shield them from seizure as a result of the liquidation, bankruptcy and receivership of the tangled companies involved.
If the Government fails to do this, I believe that in the final analysis the trust industry as we know it today will not exist very much longer. It is a dirty, tangled, smelly mess.
One of the headlines appearing in the papers today says: "Are the Trusts Just a Bust?" That headline appeared in a

Madam Speaker, I am pleased with this opportunity to speak under the provisions of Standing Order 21. My subject is Bill C-78 which was passed by the House last year in February and subsequently, after being passed by the Senate, received Royal Assent in May of the same year.
I would like to draw the attention of the House to Section 17 as it applies to a person receiving pre-retirement benefits and who is, already was or subsequently becomes a widow. If this person is receiving pre-retirement benefits under Section 17, according to the Section, the benefits this person receives as a widow must be deducted, except for retirement or disability pensions provided under the Canada Pension Plan or the Quebec Pension Plan.
Madam Speaker, in the circumstances, a woman who is widowed and is receiving pre-retirement benefits, even if her husband contributed to the Quebec Pension Plan all his life, is penalized because her pre-retirement benefits are subtracted.
I think this has created a special problem, since widows, women who worked with their husbands, are being penalized. People who have become disabled or are retired do not have equivalent amounts deducted from their pre-retirement benefits, but as soon as a woman is widowed, she loses certain amounts under the provisions of Section 17. Madam Speaker, I would therefore ask the Minister of Labour to look into this matter and amend the Act so as to avoid penalizing women who become widows.

Madam Speaker, there is no question it is quite evident that our farmers are among the most productive in the world. In fact it is generally agreed that they are the unsung heroes of the so-called war against inflation.
There is no question as well that Canadians do indeed receive a tremendous deal when they line up at check out counters of supermarkets and other food stores. Those who complain about the high cost of various food products are indeed missing the point when you consider that, in Britain, families spend about 30 per cent of disposable income on food. In West Germany it is 33 per cent, and in Japan food costs are 40 per cent of disposable income. In Canada we spend little more than 18 per cent of disposable income on food.
Beset by high interest rates, escalating costs, and low prices, it is remarkable that our agricultural community is able to compete in world markets. In spite of this, many consumers downgrade farmers the minute food prices increase, no matter how little. Perhaps it is time that all of us begin to understand that, unlike many other countries, we are able to buy what we want and at prices that are among the cheapest in the world.
Our farmers deserve more recognition and credit for the tremendous job they are doing. Therefore I call upon the Government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) to recognize seriously and to deal seriously with their problems in the forthcoming budget by providing all assistance necessary to keep our farmers and food producers solvent. Otherwise the farm population will decrease even move to the further detriment of our economy and of the food industry in particular.

subtopic: ELIGIBILITY OF MUNICIPALITIES FOR RRAP PROGRAM
ELIGIBILITY OF MUNICIPALITIES FOR RRAP PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, commonly referred to as RRAP, has been an unprecedented success, thanks to the project officers and other CMHC employees who helped to set up the project. For instance, in the riding of Levis alone, 117 homes were improved during the first eight months of 1982, $491,000 were lent under the program and $379,000 will be paid to citizens in the form of grants.
We feel, however, that the rural side of the program should be broadened. At the present time, only rural municipalities with fewer than 2,500 people are eligible for rural RRAP. Otherwise, they come under the urban RRAP, and the procedure for obtaining a grant is far more laborious. We feel that the Canadian Government should immediately make municipalities with up to 10,000 inhabitants eligible for rural RRAP, and plan to raise the ceiling even more in the years to come.
April 12, 1983

We are aware that if rural RRAP were offered to all municipalities, the costs involved would be astronomical. We would like to remind the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) that the program has a direct job-creating effect on a sector that has suffered considerably, namely, the construction industry. This would certainly be a welcome addition to the budget speech on April 19.

Madam Speaker, yesterday in this House the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said "the economy is performing well".
"Performing well" with Statistics Canada just releasing figures that 1,658,000 people are unemployed, with some
475,000	persons out of work and discouraged from even looking for a job.
"Performing well" with business bankruptcies in Canada up 55 per cent and farm bankruptcies up 111 per cent over one year ago.
"Performing well" with 40,000 of our young people being forced to leave their Canada to find work.
"Performing well" when the pillows of hundreds of women are wet with tears because UIC has run out and there is no money for clothes or sufficient food for the kids.
The Prime Minister must be living in a different world, or perhaps he meant the "economy is performing well" for exMinisters like Mr. Buchanan and Mr. Gillespie, and for Senator Pitfield. Certainly the economy is not performing well for two million unemployed, for hundreds of young people about to leave university or high school, for our businesses or our farms.
I urge the Prime Minister to get out among the people and to heed the aftermath of a similar statement from a well-to-do person in France when told that the people were hungry and had no bread. "Let them eat cake!" she said.
"The economy is performing well," our Prime Minister says. Shame!

Madam Speaker, on May 1, 1983, the CNR is scheduled to go ahead with the system-wide lay-offs that it announced in January. At Tran-scona Shops this means that a couple of hundred young railroaders with families, mortgages, and a will to work, are facing a permanent lay-off. Yet they also know that this layoff could be significantly reduced if the CNR were to build the 900 coal cars it needs, in its own shops, as it is now capable of
doing in Transcona, for instance. This has been their hope, and mine, that, through a decision of the CNR to build all or a portion of the cars itself, jobs could be saved.
With May 1 not far away, and in view of the fact that speculation about the coal car contract has lingered for months, I suggest to the Minister of Transport that he ask CNR, in all fairness, to make up its mind so that, whatever the case may be, people will at least know what is going on and will be able to plan accordingly. People whose economic wellbeing is dependent upon such decisions deserve to be informed earlier than at the last possible minute.
Having said that, I nevertheless want to repeat my contention that the lay-offs are unnecessary in any case and will turn out to be an example of tragic shortsightedness on the part of the Government, whose failure to mandate the CNR to plan for the long-term, instead of responding to short-term budget considerations, hurts not just CN workers but the whole country. If there were any economic sense on the other side we would be talking about whether more people were to be hired to build coal cars, and not about reducing the effect of an unnecessary and short sighted lay-off. There is, after all, plenty of work to be done.

Madam Speaker, I want to raise a point which I believe is timely, with the second Commonwealth Conference on Delegated Legislation being held in Ottawa this week.
Over the course of the life of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments where the committee has been charged with the responsibility of inquiring into the legality of regulations passed by the Government, a problem has arisen. Often our Committee counsel makes recommendations which indicate that, in his opinion, actions taken by the Government are illegal. The response the Committee has had in the past often stated that the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) had been asked and had given a legal opinion which indicated the Government's actions were entirely legal. When the Committee asked for an explanation of that, the Committee was told the opinion was privileged because of a solicitor-client relationship, and it would not be given an explanation.
On January 13, 1977, the then Minister of Justice, Mr. Basford, wrote to the Committee to indicate that, in future, Departments would be given the responsibility of explaining to the Committee why it was that their actions were legal. Unfortunately, in recent days we found the Government
