subtopic: UREA FORMALDEHYDE FOAM INSULATION-UNITED STATES COURT RULING
UREA FORMALDEHYDE FOAM INSULATION-UNITED STATES COURT RULING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the decision in the United States Court of Appeal overturning the ban on urea formaldehyde foam insulation used in the insulation of residential property brings to the fore the problems of all sorts of Canadians who have taken advantage of the CHIP program and insulated their homes with this foam. In some cases the foam, improperly installed, has caused health problems, but in the vast majority of cases, as was found in the Court of Appeal in the United States, there is no health hazard.
The effect, unfortunately, of the ban on urea formaldehyde foam insulation and the subsequent publicity has been to make those homes where there is no health problem totally unsaleable and unmortgageable, and the owners of those homes have suffered enormous financial loss. The Government's $5,000 grant is of little assistance. The foam cannot be removed for $5,000 and, unless a home can be certified foam-free, no mortgage company will lend, few buyers will purchase, and then only at a significant discount.
This House must deal with the problem which the ban on urea formaldehyde foam insulation has created for home owners, by certifying those homes where there is no health problem to be safe, and by guaranteeing the homes and occupants against any health hazard.

Madam Speaker, women in this country still only earn 60 per cent of the average wage of men because they are restricted to job ghettoes, yet the Government states that it has a commitment to affirmative action, which is a plan to rectify this systematic discrimination. What is absent is any results from the policies of the Government. In fact there is only one affirmative action plan resulting from this policy right across the country.
I want to refer briefly to the memo that was issued a year ago in Winnipeg that directed the local affirmative action consultants not to take any action in this area. It is time that the Government started to respond and to answer some tough questions about affirmative action. How many contracts have they signed? How many firms have been visited? Has the action on affirmative action that was promised a year ago, resulted in anything? If there are no results we can only conclude that the Government has no concern about the incomes of women and no real commitment to affirmative action.

subtopic: EFFECT OF COURT RULING ON NARCOTIC CONTROL ACT

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: EFFECT OF COURT RULING ON NARCOTIC CONTROL ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, let me bring to the attention of the House of Commons, particularly of the Minister of Justice, a recent decision of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, that affects the enforcement of the Narcotic Control Act. The Supreme Court of Nova Scotia held that the so-called onus provision under the Narcotic Control Act was unconstitutional by virtue of the provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. This will allow drug traffickers to avoid the responsibility placed on them under that provision of the law in relation to charges of trafficking in narcotics and other illicit drugs. This will have an adverse effect on the administration and enforcement of the Narcotic Control Act.
I hope the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) will examine this decision very carefully and bring before this House of Commons, at the earliest opportunity, legislation that will correct the effect of this court decision. I do not think when this House of Commons passed the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms it intended to benefit drug traffickers. I think the Minister of Justice can take action to remedy this result.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister who yesterday, in response to a question posed by my colleague from Lethbridge-Foothills, stated that the young people of Canada should look at the reality of statistics rather than at the gloom that is forecast by the Opposition. Since the recession which we are suffering began in this country, 401,000 young people have lost
April 12, 1983

their jobs, including 10,000 people last month. There are fewer young people employed now that at any time since 1973. Given these realities, how does the Prime Minister expect anyone in this country to believe that the economy is performing well? What rate of unemployment does the Prime Minister believe we have to reach before he will say that the economy is not performing well?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member will recollect that yesterday, in the exchange with the Minister of Finance, he quoted several statistics indicating the increase in job creation and the increase in productivity. I gave some statistics indicating an increase in the Gross Domestic Product over the past several months, the past three months I believe.
It is obvious that, if you look at the figures of high unemployment and the figures of still high interest rates, you can take a pessimistic view of the future. The Minister of Finance, other Ministers and the Government are not taking that pessimistic view. They are saying that there are signs of improvement. It is these signs of improvement to which the Minister of Finance and I referred yesterday. You can always look at these signs of improvement, hang your head and say it will get worse. We say it is going to get better, and we intend to have a budget that will make things better faster.

Madam Speaker, with the rate of unemployment we face in this country, particularly as it relates to young people who will be coming into the workforce very soon from the schools of the nation, I cannot understand how anyone in his right mind would suggest that the economy is working well. The Prime Minister is desensitized to the plight of Canadians who are unemployed. Indeed, it permeates the press in this country, and the Government. They have become insensitive toward the human tragedy occurring across the country in terms of those who are facing unemployment.
The Government has taken the position that it is going to tough out this recession and place the consequences on the backs of the unemployed. Is this the attitude that the Government is taking in its new budget, that the economy is performing well, when one out of every five young people in the country is out of work?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member refers to the necessity to have an open mind, and questions whether the economy is working well. I wonder if his open mind is working well. He accuses the Government of being insensitive to these problems. Not only are we not insensitive to them, we deplore the situation and we have done a great deal about it. We spent more than $2.5 billion in the June budget and in the October-November announcement of the Minister. More than a billion of this was addressed to creating jobs and helping to create skills among the young people.
Oral Questions
It is obviously not a matter of the Government being insensitive. On the contrary, these figures indicate that we are not only telling the people that we are trying to provide jobs for them, but we are not taking the attitude that we are going to tough it out. If we were, we would be looking at the Opposition and saying, "Let us just talk about the doom and gloom". We are presenting programs. We did in the June budget, and in November. We will do it again next week in the coming budget, to create jobs, to create the skills and create the infrastructure which will help the economy pull out of its very serious situation.
I repeat, the Hon. Member's mind must not be working very well if he has not seen this, if he just wants to look at the bad side of the economy and not look at the positive indicators that everybody is recognizing. It may not be a great future, but it can be if we decide to make it so.

Madam Speaker, for a country that has had the poorest growth rate of all of the OECD nations, it is difficult for any of us to try to be dispassionate and look at these figures in a constructive way to find anything to give us any hope for the future, with this Government in control.
I want to ask the Prime Minister a question in relation to youth unemployment. In 1977 the Prime Minister told young people of Canada at the University of Toronto, "If they don't like it here, let them find another country. If it is just a job you want, my heart does not bleed for you." In view of the fact that in 1977 there were 411,000 young Canadians out of work and now we have 658,000 young people out of work, I want to ask the Prime Minister if this is the current continuation of his philosophy and the Government's philosophy, that their hearts do not bleed for the young people of this nation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member is reaching to 1977 to talk about my philosophy. I would be very interested to compare my philosphy in that exchange I had at the University of Toronto or at any one of the halls of university with that of the Hon. Member. I was telling the students that the Government could not sign a blank cheque and guarantee them their future; that we could not guarantee them jobs; that if they wanted that, we would have to have a totalitarian state in which indeed we could direct students to study this and do that, and that was my philosophy. I am surprised that it seems unacceptable to the Hon. Member. Is he holding, and is his Party holding, that the Government owes a job to everyone and that the Government should be directing every student into every particular department so that he would have a guaranteed job in some part of the country regardless of his freedom to move? I would

be very surprised if that were the philosophy of the Hon. Member.
Instead of digging back to 1977 why doesn't he dig back a little bit into his own ingenuity and ask himself what his philosophy is on this matter.

REQUEST FOR ADVICE FROM PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is also addressed to the Prime Minister. In terms of our philosophy I think it is very clear that in our Party we believe that, in a country with the riches and the scope of Canada's, every Canadian should be able to find a job.
In terms of youth unemployment, we are talking about a lost generation. We know that one out of four young men in Canada under the age of 25 is out of work. As a parent, what practical advice does the Prime Minister have to offer our sons and our daughters who want to earn their independence and pay their own way? What practical message can they take to cope with a situation that looks very bleak to them?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ADVICE FROM PRIME MINISTER

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is addressed to the Prime Minister.
In view of the Prime Minister's statement Monday that the economy is "performing well", how does he describe the circumstances facing the half million Canadians whose jobs have disappeared and who will never return to the work bench or never return to the mine site or never return to their ordinary job because those jobs have gone forever? What hope does he offer them?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, how I describe that is as a very regrettable situation. Canada is caught up in a world-wide depression, recession, whatever you want to call it. We are part of the trading nations of the world, and we are doing our best in order to make sure that jobs will be created. I repeat, we have spent more than $2'/2 billion in order to do that. We are announcing projects every week. There will be more in the budget next week. We are not telling people that things are going to get miraculously better overnight in Canada just because the Opposition wills it, if the rest of the world does not enter into the recovery process at the same time as we do.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT TARGET BE SET FOR UNEMPLOYMENT REDUCTION
REQUEST THAT TARGET BE SET FOR UNEMPLOYMENT REDUCTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister has just referred to what is appropriately described as a world-wide recession. I have a question for him precisely in this context.
There are two other industrial countries, Sweden and Japan, which have unemployment levels of 3 per cent, which is one-quarter the unemployment level in this country. The other characteristic that these other two countries have, however, unlike the Government of Canada, is that the Governments of Sweden and Japan have declared a national emergency in terms of unemployment being at 3 per cent in their lands. On the eve of the budget, given the human cost of unemployment in Canada, given the economic cost of about $1 billion a month in unemployment insurance alone, will the Prime Minister give his assurances that the Government will say there is an emergency in terms of unemployment, and set specific growth targets for 1983 in terms of guaranteeing, in terms of its targets, in terms of bringing in special programs, a bringing down of the level of unemployment by a certain percentage by the end of this year?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT TARGET BE SET FOR UNEMPLOYMENT REDUCTION

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Government of the two countries I have referred to have not talked in slogans, they have not made vague promises in the past, they have acted. That is why, even today in the worldwide recession the Prime Minister is talking about, they have only 3 per cent unemployment.
My question to the Prime Minister is in terms of action. He did promise a while ago that we would have in Canada what my Party has talked about for a long time, namely, an industrial strategy. The Prime Minister said in 1980 that the Government, and I quote him, must not remain "a passive referee" but instead become "an active player" in the economy. Just before the Parliamentary recess the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said the opposite. He said the Government should intervene only when and where the private sector tells it to. Will the Prime Minister clear up this contradiction? Does the Government believe that it ought not to remain passive, or is it going to do now what the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said, simply let the private
April 12, 1983

sector do what it will and let the chips fall where they may, even if that means two million unemployed Canadians?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I don't think the Hon. Member would be suggesting that the private sector itself reflects a situation where there are
1,600,000	unemployed. The Hon. Member knows that the private sector, which includes the employers, the investors and so on, has been having a difficult time of it as well. Therefore it is not for their love of unemployment that they think the private sector can do a job. I have said many times before that this Government has a philosophy which permits Government intervention in some cases. For instance, we have made that quite clear in areas like the creation of Petro-Canada, and our national energy policy, and so on.
In the overwhelming majority of areas we say the jobs should be created by the private sector, and it is the business of the Government to try to make sure that the appropriate social legislation is in place to make sure that the people who have to be helped are assisted. But, by and large, the jobs have to come from the private sector. Therefore the private sector has to have good confidence in the future of the economy, in the way it will be conducted, and in the possibility of investing soundly in order that jobs be created.

Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister knows as well as the people on this side of the House that he did not answer the question at all. No one is saying that the majority of Canadians, now and in the foreseeable future, won't be employed in the private sector. What we are asking the Government is whether, in the context of a mixed economy, it is going to live up to its own commitment to provide an industrial strategy, which is a different kind of matter entirely.
I want to ask the Prime Minister if he is standing by his old campaign promise, or is he going in the direction of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce? Will he give Canadians a sense of hope, a sense of optimism about the future, by saying the Government will play an active role in setting investment priorities in the economy so we can get more long-range jobs which Canadians desperately need?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member uses the term "mixed economy", which is the one this Government has been following. If he needs examples of Government intervention and direction given to the economy, he could look to his right and he would find too many examples to please them. Here is a case where the Government was giving direction to the economy, proposing solutions, and what happens? Pawn shops.

more than we have done in the past. As the Prime Minister has said, we have taken numerous measures in that regard. We are trying to see whether we could do even more, but at the same time one should not believe that there is a kind of cure-all that one budget can bring forward.

Madam Speaker, I believe I have about five minutes left in which to complete my remarks. This morning before the luncheon break, I covered many phases of the Bill and related many of the details pertaining to Astra Trust. It is interesting to note whom we have seen making representations before the House of Commons on the matter of Astra Trust and other trust company matters. I do not believe we heard anything, at any time during the tortuous events involving Astra Trust and ReMor, from the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls (Mr. McBain) or the Hon. Member for Welland (Mr. Parent). However, we did hear from the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid), the Hon. Member for Erie (Mr. Fretz), the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and from others on this side of the House whose constituents have lost money in that affair. Until the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) stood, there had been little or no representation from the Government benches to the various Ministers who had responsibility for the CDIC.
In the few minutes left to me, I would like to leave a few more questions with the House, because I believe that we should have a full inquiry, a royal commission into this whole matter involving the bankruptcy, the receivership and the difficulties of Astra Trust, ReMor, C & M Financial Services and all the other trust companies which have been involved in financial difficulties. I say that because we need the trust industry in this country. We really cannot get along without it. Unless some strong support and help is given to that industry in the period ahead, then I am afraid it will lapse and become ineffectual as a source of financial funds.
One of the things in the Astra Trust matter which has intrigued me is the conduct of the former Minister of Finance. Two of his officials from the Department of Insurance had to be subpoenaed by a Speaker's warrant to ensure that they would appear before a committee of the Ontario Legislature. Both of the Ministers who have been responsible in the conduct of the matter involving Astra Trust have laboured again and again to try to dissociate the federal Government from
April 12, 1983

that matter. In fact, the former Minister of State for Finance has said that we should not try to link Astra Trust and ReMor unconditionally. He said that the nature of the inquiries is different, that the RCMP is investigating Astra Trust and that the Province of Ontario is investigating ReMor. He has given no information to us at all but, rather, has advised his officials, when summoned before the provincial committee, not to give evidence to assist the committee in coming to a resolution.
Then we had the spectacle of the Minister standing here today and saying that there is no connection, that he wants the Minister in the provincial House to provide him with evidence of some connection before the Government will consider reimbursing those who were gutted by the ReMor operation, before they are to receive any funds from the federal Government. I think it is deplorable, degrading and disgusting, and it is unbecoming of the federal Government of this country.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise to speak today on Bill C-142, because there was a great deal of discussion and study concerning this particular matter of deposit insurance at the time of the investigation into bank profits. As indicated earlier by the Minister and by other Hon. Members, the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, of which I had the privilege and honour of being Chairman, did bring a recommendation back to the House and to the Government that the limits of deposit insurance be raised from the present limit of $20,000 to $60,000. Subsequently, the Minister indicated that he intended to do just that and introduced Bill C-142, indicating at the time of introduction that the legislation would be applied as of the date of introduction which, to my understanding, was January 17 of this year. Therefore, we are now discussing legislation which I very strongly urge should be passed, if not today, at the earliest possible opportunity, although hopefully today. This legislation would then raise the limit, retroactively back to January 17, to $60,000.
Questions raised in a Private Member's Bill presented earlier by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) would suggest that the limit should be raised to $100,000 as opposed to $60,000. At that time I spoke and indicated that I did not agree with that increase. I raised a number of reasons at that time and I will reiterate those as I go through my comments today.
First, the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs considered the question of the adequacy of the coverage of deposit insurance. Since the deposit insurance limits which we now have were established in the mid-sixties, it was clear that inflation had badly eroded the coverage which was available to depositors under that Act. As a result, our solution was to inflation-exhaust the limit of $20,000 and to bring the global limit back to a level such that the real level of protection would be the same as it was when the limit was established in the mid-sixties. To do that would raise the level of deposit insurance coverage to approximately $60,000.
After extensive discussion by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), the Hon. Member for Mississauga
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
North (Mr. Fisher), the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middle-sex (Mr. Ferguson), the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) and others, it was found that all of these Hon. Members were, to a greater or lesser degree, of the opinion that $60,000 was the appropriate figure because it simply restored the real value of that coverage. There were, of course, certain Hon. Members who believed that a slightly higher figure would be appropriate. Others, quite honestly, were of the opinion that something lower than $60,000 would be appropriate. After due discussion and deliberation in the Committee, we were ultimately able to come to a consensual agreement that $60,000 was the appropriate figure. We therefore recommended that figure in the study on bank profits to which I earlier referred. As I have said, this Bill raises the coverage to a level today which is the equivalent in real terms of the coverage when it was established in the mid-1960s. In my opinion, it provides for adequate coverage.
One reason it is essential that these limits be raised is that with today's Registered Retirement Savings Plans and other forms of savings, which are so necessary today to protect the retirement of Canadians, it is important to have enough coverage such that individuals do not have to spread small deposits among a large number of institutions in order to protect their savings. Savings of $20,000 can be exceeded very rapidly in a Registered Retirement Savings Plan, with its compound interest and so on. It is important that we not force individuals to maintain a large number of small deposits but make it easier for them to maintain their deposits in fewer accounts. The $60,000 limit would certainly provide for that.
Many individuals who have retirement funds in place now, especially those in my riding, have contacted me in recent weeks to ask whether or not their retirement savings are indeed covered by the legislation. The Minister has indicated earlier that those who have their savings in Greymac Trust and Seaway Trust would be covered by the legislation since it would be retroactive to January 17. Since the receivership did not occur at that time, the deposits in those institutions would indeed be covered by the new legislation.
Some questions were raised in the House earlier by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South as to the certainty with which the Minister holds that view. I am sure the Minister will clarify that question at a later point in this debate. The issue at hand now concerns the fact that there is a great deal of confusion existing in my riding, and 1 am sure in other ridings in the country as well, about whether individuals who have deposits in excess of $20,000 in these institutions which have experienced trouble in recent months are covered by the new limits of deposit insurance. That confusion must be cleared up.
A second real problem exists irrespective of whether the new limits will apply retroactively. It concerns the fact that receivers of these institutions to which we have referred have indicated to some of my constituents who have retirement savings plans which are generating income for them now for their retirement that until the legislation is passed, even though the

April 12, 1983
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
Government intends to cover amounts up to $60,000, the individual will have the right to receive only $20,000 maximum should any of the certificates of deposit come due, minus the interest that has accrued in income to these individuals back to the date of the receivership.
For example, if an individual had $50,000 or $60,000 in certificates in one of these institutions which came due on May 1, he would be given $20,000 less the interest that has been paid for the period of two months or three months. The other $40,000 would remain in receivership and unavailable to the individual depositor. As a result, the reinvestment of that money would not be possible. Consequently, the income stream that is generated by the savings that the individual has accumulated would fall dramatically in the ensuing months.
If the legislation was not passed until September or October, those individuals who have contacted me in my riding would have to live on greatly reduced incomes since their savings would not be available to generate the income on which they are living. For that reason, regardless of whether the legislation is retroactive, which the Minister's comments make me confident it is, it is very important that the legislation is enacted as soon as possible to ensure that these term certificates can be reinvested as they become due in order to generate the income that many individuals are depending on for their retirement income. For that reason alone, I believe it is imperative that the House not be complacent about the passage of this legislation and pass it now with all the diligence which has been shown toward the legislation.
This is a relatively simple piece of legislation which does not require a great deal of analysis and study. The Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs has conducted that study and recommended to the House in good conscience that the limit be raised to $60,000. Therefore, I would ask the House to act on this recommendation and pass the legislation immediately.
It will certainly reduce the concern that many of my constituents have expressed to me, not only about the security of their savings but their ability to generate the necessary income to enable them to carry on their daily lives. I do not believe there is any reason to hold this legislation up any longer. It has been carefully considered and its contents have been recommended to the House by all parties on the Committee. I hope the House will act on this legislation expeditiously, put it through all three stages today, send it to the other place for consideration and give it Royal Assent within a short period of time.
1 wish to comment briefly on the opinion that I and I believe other Members of the Finance Committee shared about the proposal to raise the limit to $100,000. When we examined this issue in Committee we rejected the idea of providing amounts greater than $60,000 as well as the amount of $100,000 specifically recommended by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands. It was the view that $60,000 is an amount that allows individuals to spread their investments efficiently in one institution in different types of savings vehicles or in a number of institutions.
As the Minister indicated earlier, an individual may have a savings account which is covered up to $60,000 as well as a Registered Retirement Savings Plan account which is covered up to the same amount. An individual may then have up to $120,000 covered in those two accounts in any one institution. Furthermore, an individual could potentially have up to $240,000 in two institutions, and it causes very little inconvenience to an individual to cover the size of his deposit and protect his savings with federal insurance. In addition, an individual and his or her spouse could have a joint account which would allow another $60,000 to be covered. Therefore, two individuals having separate accounts and a joint account would have coverage exceeding $500,000, which is far in excess of what the average Canadian will ever have in any of these institutions. Therefore, $60,000 coverage is entirely adequate for the average Canadian and, indeed, the far above average income Canadian.
What are the implications of raising these limits? As they are raised from $20,000 to $60,000, it will be necessary for the Deposit Insurance Fund to include larger amounts to offset the potential liability that exists with the insurance coverage. That will mean each financial institution will have to pay higher premiums into the fund. After all, the insurance coverage ultimately comes from premiums paid by the financial institutions. This will mean that individual Canadian savers will either have to earn lower rates of return on their deposits- because that is where the money will come from to pay premiums-or borrowers will have to pay higher rates on loans in order to make up the additional premiums. I do not think that is necessary, Mr. Speaker. If we limit the amount to $60,000 maximum, the premium increases can be minimized and all Canadians can receive the kind of effective protection they need.
In addition, as we raise premiums we have to ask ourselves what are we doing and on whom are we putting the cost? All institutions will have to pay in accordance with the deposit liabilities they have. This means that large, efficient institutions will be paying the lion's share of the premiums in order to protect small, inefficient and improperly run institutions.
What we are doing by raising these limits excessively and requiring that the premiums be raised to fund this insurance is requiring well run, efficient institutions to subsidize potential losers, the poorly run institutions. This would give the poorly run institutions a competitive edge which they would not otherwise have vis-a-vis well run institutions. We are not encouraging institutions to be prudent and well managed when we raise the amount of insurance that will be available to them. I do not think we should provide full insurance coverage for all deposits in all institutions. There should be an incentive on the part of the institution to be well managed and prudent and to make that fact known to the public. I do not think you should place all institutions in the position of having to subsidize the losses that may occur as a result of events such as those we have seen recently with regard to the provincial trust companies that have faced difficulty.
April 12, 1983

I have a couple of comments in closing. This whole issue of deposit insurance and the issues we are facing with regard to ReMor and Astra Trust raised by the Hon. Member a moment ago, and the issues that have been raised by Greymac, Seaway Trust and others in recent times, raise a much more fundamental issue in this country than simply whether or not insurance coverage is adequate for certain financial institutions or whether these financial institutions are being run properly. What we have I would say, in my view, is an archaic, fragmented system of financial institutions in Canada.
It seems to me the time is right, in fact it has been right for quite some time, for a review as to what the powers of these financial institutions should be, where they should be able to operate and how we can stimulate greater competition between institutions. I suggest the way to do that is to bring forward a revision to the Trust Companies Act and the Loan Companies Act at the earliest possible opportunity. We should at least refer that matter to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs so we can get at it.
There are other financial institutions which have also indicated their desire to have their enabling legislation reviewed; the insurance companies, for instance. Over the years I have been in communication with co-operatives. They have indicated they would like to have some enabling legislation at the federal level allowing them to qualify for deposit insurance and to operate outside the confines of one Province. There are some others.
Years back when I was a public servant at the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, a very good friend of mine and an eminent scholar, Dr. Phil Anisman who is now at York University, completed an intensive and comprehensive study of a national securities act which would start a move into a national regime of regulating securities. This would expand Canada's capital markets and make it easier for firms and individuals who wish to start businesses to raise equity capital.
These are the kinds of broader questions which have to be addressed within the context of financial markets and institutions, in addition to the very important legislation we are dealing with here today. It seems to me the time has come for us to be looking at the broader question of financial institutions in this country. We completed the review of the Bank Act, and I think we did an admirable job of revising that Act two years ago. But I think the job has only just started. We have to move on to trust and loan companies, which are badly in need of legislative review, and to insurance companies and co-operatives, such as credit unions and the Caisses populaires, and finally to the whole question of a national securities act. We have our plate full for many years to come and I think it is time we got down to business on these things.

speechtext: Order, please. Are there any questions?

Mr. Speaker, does the Hon. Member think the Government should structure a committee of the House to look into the proposed loan and trust companies act and the white paper concerning that together with the Canada Deposit
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
Insurance Corporation, particularly in view of the fact that we have had some real supervisory problems concerning trust companies as evidenced by the losses in Greymac, Seaway and Crown? Does the Hon. Member think that is the way to proceed, bearing in mind it is the report of the Finance Committee with respect to bank profits that suggested the Canada deposit insurance limit be increased to $60,000?

Mr. Speaker, those of us who are members of the Finance Committee have for some time now been saying precisely what the Hon. Member for Mississauga South has been saying. Trust company legislation should be referred. We have asked that it be referred. I am sure the Minister will at the earliest opportunity refer that legislation to our committee or introduce legislation in the House for first and second reading. Perhaps we can get it that way. I am sure members of the Committee would be prepared to undertake the task of reviewing that legislation, making recommendations on how we could proceed at the earliest opportunity. I think that would be appropriate. I think we are capable of doing a fairly first-rate job of making those recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, bearing in mind that members of the Committee have not been satisfied over the past three years with the management of the Department of Insurance, particularly with respect to the insurance companies Pitts, Strathcona and Caledonia with respect to Astra and ReMor, and now with respect to Greymac Mortgage, Seaway Mortgage and so on, which is clearly a sleeping policeman operation, does the Hon. Member believe that the management capacity of the Department of Insurance should be specifically referred either to the standing committee or a special committee of this House?

Mr. Speaker, I am of a contrary mind to the Hon. Member on that particular question, primarily because I have not, in my analysis of the situation we have been facing, been troubled by the adequacy of the scrutiny done by the federal Department of Insurance. However, I have become very concerned with the adequacy of the scrutiny given by provincial regulatory bodies with respect to trust and loan companies. I am very concerned with that. I know that concern is shared by Members of the provincial legislature and by others who have looked into this. However, I would stop very far short of making condemnations of the federal Department of Insurance, which I think has done an excellent job in dealing with the regulatory problems it has faced. It has done an excellent job with its limited manpower. I suggest that that operation has been given its mandate and its regulatory power. It has done a very good job of dealing with the problems that have come before the country in the area to which we are referring. I would not say the same, of course, with regard to its provincial counterparts.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to raise a couple of questions with the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
April 12, 1983
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
Evans). A number of times during his presentation he mentioned the inquiry carried out by the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs into bank profits. He will recall that on a number of occasions concerns regarding the banks' high risk exposure in terms of sovereign loans were raised in the Committee.
Has the Hon. Member given any thought to the possibility that increasing the depositors' insurance, as we are doing today, from $20,000 to $60,000 might encourage the financial institutions to become even more exposed as a result of this increase? I base this question on recent studies done in the United States which have found that to be the case in the American financial scene. Has the Hon. Member given any thought to the Canadian scene in that regard?

Yes, Mr. Speaker. In fact, I mentioned in my speech, if the Hon. Member had been listening a little more carefully, that one of the problems with raising deposit insurance significantly above the level that we have recommended was that it did indeed take some pressure off the institution to be financially prudent. However, I would suggest that it is not appropriate for us to reject the increase in deposit insurance as a means of ensuring prudent management of financial institutions. That can be done through the regulatory vehicles available to us. That includes the Inspector General of Banks and the Superintendent of Insurance. As I said, these two arms of Government, these two regulatory bodies, have done a very good job.
During the study of bank profits, the Inspector General of Banks raised a concern. It is on the public record. There was concern with regard to some of the issues raised by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap that we should be looking at that issue. Indeed, we did look at that issue relatively carefully. We did make some recommendations on capital adequacy and the other issues that have just been referred to. We did look at that and made recommendations. To the best of my knowledge, the Inspector General of Banks is watching that issue very closely. From all the reports I have, it seems that Canadian banks have been able to weather this storm in a very successful fashion.

Mr. Speaker, I would certainly like to debate that last comment of the Hon. Member, but this is not the time or the place. The Hon. Member went on at some length about the necessity for Opposition co-operation in terms of quick passage of this Bill. He stated that the Bill has been before the House for some time and it is time we wrapped it up. I believe that is the intent of the House. It is certainly the intent of my Party.
Can the Hon. Member explain why it was, when his House Leader brought forward the 13 Bills that had high priority for moving through this House, this Bill was not included in that list?

Mr. Speaker, it is certainly not my job to recommend what is priority and what is not priority to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard). I can assure him that in my discussions with the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove), who brought this Bill forward originally and
brought it to the House today for second reading, it was clear that the Bill had priority in his mind all along. That is reflected by the fact that it is before the House now for debate on the second day after we came back from the Easter break.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) quite often has some good ideas. He is one of the more thoughtful Members opposite. Of the two suggestions that he made today, I certainly concur with the first one, that a Committee of Parliament make a detailed study of the legislation affecting financial institutions.
If the Trust Companies Act were referred to the Committee, I am sure there would be no problem with the Official Opposition, if this session of Parliament ended and another one began, in bringing the legislation back to the Committee at the same stage, as was done with the Bank Act. That makes a lot of sense when something as complex as the Trust Companies Act is being studied.
The Hon. Member's second idea dealt with national securities legislation. When he said that, it rang a bell. I must say that it got my back up. This is something of a new idea. Can he explain briefly exactly what he means. Is there to be federal Government licensing of brokers and investment counsellors? Will there be federal control over stock exchanges? What exactly did he have in mind?

I did not know we were still on questions. I was expecting this to be a speech that the Hon. Member was commencing. There is a very large document which I think is entitled "A National Securities Act" which would provide for centralized regulatory procedures for the issuance of and dealing in securities from coast to coast.
As the Hon. Member knows, the Province of Ontario has the Ontario Securities Act. It established the standard by which most other provincial Governments established their securities acts. There are very real differences. Stock exchanges in Calgary, Vancouver, Montreal and Toronto do not operate in precisely the same way. The listing conditions are not the same. I would refer to the study by Dr. Anisman, published by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs under the title of the Minister's name. It is about that thick. It is a very well researched and well documented piece of work that is highly commended.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak on this Bill which increases the present coverage for depositors from $20,000 to $60,000. I want to assure the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) that this Party is all for that Bill and has been for a long time. We would like to see speedy passage of the Bill. However, I disagree with the Hon. Member when he says there is no blame on the federal Department of Insurance or on the Government for the fiasco in which we find ourselves as far as the Deposit Insurance Corporation is concerned.
Let us hearken back to some of the old publications of 1980 and look at what was said with regard to ReMor and Astra, Astra in particular. In October 1979 Astra Trust had been
April 12, 1983

under increasingly close supervision by the federal Department of Insurance for at least two years. That was prior to 1979. We are still waiting for them to come up to $60,000 of protection, which only covers inflation to this date.
Virtually from the day that Astra started to operate, it was being investigated. The company was founded primarily through the efforts of the two men, a Niagara Falls businessman named Carlo Montemurro, and a Welland lawyer named Patrick Luciani, but only after three years of negotiation with the Department of Insurance, the federal body that regulates trust companies. The Department of Insurance was reluctant to grant Astra Trust a licence for a number of reasons. One was that Carlo Montemurro had attempted to get an Ontario trust company charter and had been turned down. You can see that we must get our act together between the Ontario Government, the provincial Governments, and the federal Government, as far as trust companies are concerned. One of the reasons was, and I quote:
-Carlo Montemurro had attempted to get an Ontario trust Company charter and been turned down, for reasons the provincial Government has not made public.
A second was that Montemurro, a bouncy 46-year-old former hockey player, had been involved with the Canadian operations of Investors Overseas Services before that company went bankrupt, leaving investors around the world holding the bag for $224 million.
And perhaps most serious, Montemurro also owned an investment company called C & M Financial Consultants, which operated in effect as a mortgage broker, raising money and investing it in mortgages. Since the trust company would be doing essentially the same thing, the federal regulators were concerned .... Superintendent of Insurance and the civil servant Finally responsible for issuing Astra Trust's charter: "We didn't feel the people concerned should be running two companies in the same business, especially when one was subject to federal regulation and the other was not."
Yet somehow the federal regulators overcame those misgivings and granted Astra Trust a charter and a licence to operate in February of 1977.
This is now April of 1983 and there was six years during which we and the federal Government knew this type of thing was going on, and yet the Government did not see fit even to bring in legislation such as the Bill we are looking at now, not to mention tightening up the trust laws, which probably would take a new trust and loans Act.
As much as we support the legislation and want to see its speedy passage, we cannot stand here in and say in all seriousness that as far as the trust companies were concerned the federal Government or the federal Insurance Department was doing its job as a policing agent because we were forewarned a long time ago, long before we got caught in the web of Grey-mac, Seaway and Crown.
The Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation was brought into being in 1967 to provide protection for the deposits held by the chartered banks. The coverage at that time was $20,000 for each individual depositor and for each financial institution. At that time it was quite adequate. That figure was established some 15 years ago, so it is totally unrealistic in view of today's economic climate. As I mentioned before, $60,000 just brings us to today's rate of inflation. The proposed amount of $60,000
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
is an improvement, but I feel, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), and the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and some of the others have mentioned, that a more realistic sum would probably be $100,000, or $75,000 at the very least in case inflation takes us any further than it has today. That is where I disagree with the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre.
Inflation, high interest rates, ungovernable unemployment, our youth, 15 to 20 years old, are now looking at 20.6 per cent unemployment and the large Government deficits have contributed to our uncertain economic climate and are creating fear among individuals for their personal financial security.
The Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation provides deposit insurance to banks, federally-incorporated trust and loan companies, and most provincially-incorporated trust and loan companies. Credit unions and the other institutions are administered under provincial arrangements, as we are all aware.
There has been a need to increase the limit of deposit insurance from the original limit of $20,000 per person simply because there has been a significant increase in the level of deposits together with a decline in the purchasing power of these deposits. The current fiasco with Greymac, Seaway Trust and Crown Trust certainly points out and illustrates factually the need for an increase and the reason it has come before the House. As was pointed out, it was not an item that was on the Government House Leader's 13 important pieces of legislation, and yet those depositors are sitting out there chewing their fingernails, as was pointed out by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre.
The deposit insurance coverage underwritten by the federal Deposit Insurance Corporation in the United States has been reviewed and increased over the years to its present level of $100,000 per depositor per institution. Again, I disagree with the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre. I think it is our duty to make sure that the small additional amount that would be charged would bring it up to the $100,000 level, because it is not really that much more than what is charged for $60,000.
The limit of $20,000 per depositor per institution in Canada has not been revised, as I said, since 1967, and we all want to see it done.
Many of my own constituents have been writing or calling me over the past months asking if their interest was going to be covered, asking what is going to happen, and that was explained. I will not go into it because it was reviewed by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre, but they wanted to know when we were going to introduce legislation to increase the amount of coverage. My reply to them has been as stock a reply as those of my colleagues. It is not up to us, it is up to the Government. We are all in favour of it, and now we have finally got in on the floor. My constituents have all been extremely worried about their deposits, and they are going to be worried about them in the future after what has happened in the Ontario trust market. It has been quite evident over the past few years that the Government has not been offering these individuals the protection they require.

April 12, 1983
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
Many proposals have been suggested over the years to strengthen the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. The Consumers Association of Canada suggested again that the limit should be $100,000, which most of us on this side of the House agree with, I think, and that the confusion should be removed from the legislation to avert any crisis of confidence. That is a very difficult thing to accomplish when one looks at today's economy in general.
The Canadian Bankers' Association had suggested increasing the coverage to $40,000 with unlimited coverage for Registered Retirement Savings Plans.
With this Bill, the Government is finally taking positive steps to ensure that there will be adequate protection for depositors. Canadian investors want to be assured that their investments are protected. I do not think they care about the little bit more that it takes to protect them as far as interest is concerned. They are tired of the uncertainty, and the best way to relieve their anxiety is to provide the security the investors have a right to expect as Canadians.
Deposit insurance was originally established in the 1930s at the initiative of the United States and in Canada as well. More serious bank failures had occurred in the United States and the authorities there were afraid that there would continue to be runs on financial institutions whenever rumours arose. Thank God we have not really had that problem in Canada. But it was feared a particular institution in the United States might not be able to pay off its depositors. Here, as I said, we do not have this same worry because there has not been the same type of uncertainty, and I think the last bank failure was in the 1920s of a relatively unknown institution, according to my information.
The Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation fund is financed through premiums from its member institutions. The large, strong institutions which hold the majority of deposit are the principal source of funds for the CDIC. Again I disagree with the Hon. Member from the Government side who feels that that little bit more to be charged in premiums would hurt. Some of these financial institutions have expressed concern that their premiums would increase if the limit were increased. However, when you look at the total amount of assets and the recent increase in profits of these large banks, I have no doubt they will be able to meet the increase in their premium payments.
The deposit insurance is arranged in such a manner that the proposed $60,000 is not the total coverage available to an individual. A depositor can have a deposit in an institution with coverage at all branches of that institution, whether it is a bank or trust company, up to the maximum of $60,000. That person's spouse can also have coverage in the same bank or trust company for accounts in that individual's name up to that $60,000. As well, they can have a third joint account which is also covered. Therefore, using three different accounts, a married couple, under the $60,000 ceiling, is insured for up to a total of $180,000 in a single institution.
If we were to take that up to the $100,000 mark, we might never have to worry again, not even in a review, which in my view should be at least every three to five years.
However, like everything else the Government does, it only introduces measures after things have reached crisis proportions such as with Greymac, Seaway and Crown Trust.
I think it is a bad commentary on our free enterprise system that the Government can step in and take over such corporations. In my Province of Ontario, as we have seen, without any charges being laid, the Government walked in and took over trust companies such as Kilderkin Investments, etc., and still it has not been proven to anybody's satisfaction that there has been any fill-in. It was probably necessary but the method by which it was done leaves a lot to be desired in a country as free to operate as Canada is. Again, I think that this is a step in the right direction. If they looked at what happened to Astra some six years ago, all of this could have been averted with a trust and loans Act. A lesson should have been learned from the whole fiasco of Astra Trust which went into bankruptcy in 1980. This firm, as I said, had been under federal Government supervision virtually from the day it started in operation, but in the end many small investors lost all their money. Last week Ontario offered to pay, retroactively, some $2.8 million to ReMor investors who suffered in the 1980 collapse of that company. I hope the federal Government will consider the same type of program. We need our trust companies. We have one of the finest banking systems in the world and we do not need threats of financial collapse for any reason. I hope there are no repetitions, and I hope that the Government has learned a lesson from the ReMor and Astra incidents. They need not have happened; the warnings were there. They could not get a provincial franchise but they did get federal funding. I think that we must review the system every three to five years.
We hope that the Bill, with our support, will get speedy passage, Mr. Speaker.
