Are there any questions or comments at this time? There being no questions, we will now proceed to debate.
The Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker).

Mr. Speaker, I rise to join with others in debating the principle of Bill C-142 to amend the provisions of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act. This Party agrees that this is one Crown corporation that fulfils a worthwhile role in society. The corporation does not take away the rights of individuals who operate but acts as background insurance so that ordinary depositors in banks and trust companies may have some protection when putting their money into the hands of others.
April 12, 1983

It is a corporation that enabled our parents and grandparents to take their money out of the socks, from under the sofa, under the bed, and from the backyards and put it into financial institutions, knowing that even if there were a run on the bank they would be protected to a limit of $20,000. We have to make the point that the $60,000 limit is just a reflection of inflation and is not really an increase.
I was interested to hear the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) say that we have 132 federally incorporated companies that are members under the statutes, comprising 55 banks and 67 trust and loan companies. There are also 52 provincially incorporated companies. It is nice to know that there is a broad degree of participation, but I wonder if the Minister could indicate at some point what types of institutions are operating in the marketplace today that are not part of this insurance protection. Perhaps this debate will alert Canadians to take steps to protect themselves. That might be sufficient incentive to those companies not presently registered to bring themselves within the statute.
I think we need to know that deposit insurance amounts to $118 billion. That is a contingent liability that Parliament has agreed the Consolidated Revenue Fund should accept in the event of a depression and a massive deflation. If people wanted their money, Parliament would have to come up with $118 billion, less the assets of banking and financial institutions at that time. I do not suppose that is impossible because, of course, we have already had a depression in this country.
I was interested to hear the Minister argue, as did the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), that the $60,000 limit will result in some 78 per cent of bank deposits and 92 per cent of deposits in trust companies being covered. Why not 100 per cent, Mr. Speaker? The advantage of raising the limit to $60,000 is that people can now close out many of the $20,000 accounts they had in different banks. They can now consolidate those accounts to a limit of $60,000. If, by the mechanism of setting up accounts in different institutions, people can obtain 100 per cent protection for their financial assets, why do we not just incrase the limit automatically to 100 per cent of the deposit? It seems to me that by putting the limit at $60,000, if there is a depression we are going to injury the ordinary Canadian who puts all his savings into one account compared to the more worldly-wise or business oriented person who spreads that money over different institutions. So why not protect the innocent, rather than those who are sophisticated?
I was glad to see that this Bill will be effective as of January 17. I look forward to hearing the Minister confirm to the House and to Canadians that all those people who put money into Crown Trust and Seaway Trust will be covered. I think that is the purpose of the increase in the limit, and we agree with that.
This protection that is granted to our citizens should be seen in the same light as stabilization programs or crop insurance. It is there to protect the people from precipitous declines in economic activity or in an emergency that might cause them to
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
have less certainty or to take other courses. That is a legitimate role for Parliament to play. I can stand wholeheartedly behind the principle of the Bill, as can most Members.
This also shows that good laws pass this House quickly. I hope the Government will take this as a lesson and keep Bills short and to the point in future. Any time there is a real feud in the House it is over omnibus Bills or Bills that attach a whole bunch of amendments that affect other statutes and are undesirable in certain parts of the country. In such cases, Members have to oppose a Bill although they may agree to 75 or 80 per cent of the content.
The Bill before us today shows that if the Government brings in short Bills and addresses a problem directly, the Parties can often come to agreement. The Government sometimes accuses us of obstruction but, as you know, Mr. Speaker, 120 Bills have been passed. The average time for a Bill to pass through the House is three days. That is not bad in a country the size of this one. After a Bill is introduced it takes many weeks for people all across the country to become fully aware of it and to make their views known to their Member of Parliament so that he or she can make some input in caucus and committees and also in the House Committees. It takes time to pass Bills, and so it should in such a huge country with the diversity of interests and of language and religion that, on the surface, could split the country as they have so many other countries. The beauty of Parliament is that when a Bill is introduced, there is enough time to receive input and to achieve the compromises that make our laws acceptable to the citizens.
I hope that all Members of the House will adopt the ninth report of the Standing Committee on Procedures and Organization, Mr. Speaker. That would permit Madam Speaker to have a panel of ten chair persons who would develop expertise on certain legislative matters. Therefore, when a Bill such as the Bill on the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation came up, the chairman of that legislative committee, who would be assigned the Bill, and a small group who would work with him, would have some very real skills on that particular legislative matter. It would not interfere with the Standing Committee which would be dealing with other matters like Estimates and special inquiries into Crown Corporations. I hope that Hon. Members will accept that because I believe it would be of great help to us.
While we need to have the certainty of this Bill so that people will be able to invest their money and not have to worry about a precipitous decline in its value, let us not forget for one moment that the reason we have this Bill before us is that it is the 100 per cent predictable and logical result of the policies of the Government over the last 15 years, which, instead of proposing a program and a corresponding tax for people, proposed a program which permitted people to keep the tax low and borrowed the difference.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, in this year alone, we are, through this Parliament, injecting into the economy of Canada some $30 billion more for the programs than we are taking

April 12, 1983
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
away from the people in terms of taxation. We are taking away from the people $30 billion by way of borrowing in order to make up the difference between the cost of the program and the taxation withdrawal from people. The ordinary citizen will ultimately pay that, but for the moment we are borrowing from people with wealth, paying them a good rate of interest, then we are distributing the money among all of us citizens. That deficit, of course, Mr. Speaker, now totals over $200 billion if we add in the deficit of the Crown Corporations. That has caused an enormous inflation in the country, which in turn has led to the high interest rates, because people do believe they are entitled to a real rate of return on their money. Elistorically, it was always 2 per cent or 3 per cent. More recently, the real rate of return has been much greater. Even when the inflation rate was 12 per cent, the interest rates were 19.5 per cent in the 1981 issue of Canada Savings Bonds, which meant that people had a greater rate of return on their money in 1981 than ever, I believe, in the entire economic history of this country. And this was at a time, Mr. Speaker, when hundreds and hundreds of thousands of people were being laid off, and when the Old Age Security benefits of our senior citizens were being restricted to a 6 per cent raise in their incomes, some $180 this year. We Members of Parliament were taking something like $3,900 out of the economy. Deputy Ministers earning $100,000 were taking an extra $6,000 out of the economy. The reason we have this Bill before us is the result of those accumulated bad policies which have put every sector of our society in jeopardy.
There are, however, certain sectors we are protecting. We are protecting with this Bill those people with enough money to have a savings deposit somewhere. There are many Canadians in this country who do not have one extra cent which they can put into a safety deposit box, by way of share certificates or cash in the bank. They simply live on a hand-to-mouth basis. Again, Mr. Speaker, that is the result of the deficit, because when you borrow $30 billion from people with wealth and you pay that back to them at the end of the year, together with the accumulated interest, they become incredibly wealthy without having to take any risks or responsibility. Indeed, if they put their money in different institutions up to $60,000, the state will guarantee them 100 per cent return. Of course, that concentration of wealth is at somebody's expense, because every nation has only a certain amount of capital which it has developed and which is ongoing at any one time. When we add this to the people who already have wealth, it invariably comes out of the pocket of the ordinary working Canadian, and very often it is the farmer who is on the land, or the man who is working in the factory.
That is why I have argued time and time again, Mr. Speaker, that we need a whole new philosophy in times of high inflation. We need to have flat across-the-board settlements rather than percentage settlements, because that will bring our society closer together rather than making the rich richer and the poor poorer, and leading to a class society which gives people no chance but to go on the streets.
I would like to state clearly to anyone who might be listening across the country, that they need to be aware that they have this protection up to only $60,000. If they are anticipating depositing $100,000 in the bank, they should slit it up and put it into two different institutions, in order to have full protection. I would like to state again that we believe that the amendment of the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) was entirely reasonable at $100,000 rather than $60,000, because it is not going to be a draw on an ongoing basis in the Consolidated Revenue Fund. As I understand it, this is a self-sustaining, self-paying insurance program with the premium rate being one-thirtieth of 1 per cent from the contributing institutions, and the only time we will get involved is if there is a depression, and the only time there is going to be a depression, Mr. Speaker, is if we leave the current Government in with its philosophy of sustaining deficits. In order to protect themselves really, Canadians must get out there in the next election and defeat the Government at the polls. That means defeating the Hon. Members opposite, who are otherwise very good people with good thoughts on business, but we must defeat them individually so we can get the Government out.

Mr. Speaker, I must say this has been one of the more enjoyable days which I have spent recently in the House of Commons in terms of the quality of the debate, the seriousness of the debate and the questioning which has occurred. It has been a very positive debate. I believe Hon. Members have been really making an effort to contribute to the improvement of this legislation which is before us, and coming up with suggestions to improve subsequent legislation of a similar nature.
I listened with interest when the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) brought forth the proposal that it is high time we began to examine, via the Finance Committee, the matter of trust and loan companies in Canada. I will certainly endorse that position.
I must say, however, just to be positively critical for a moment or two, that it was January 17 when the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) brought forward this particular Bill for first reading, under a considerable amount of pressure. Pressure had mounted, particularly in the Province of Ontario, because of the problems we were having, to take some action to protect the number of depositors who were very frightened at the possibility of losing parts of their deposits because of the financial difficulties certain institutions were experiencing. When you consider that depositors' insurance rate, or amount, was set way back in 1967, it is surprising that there has not been more of an effort made by the Government to improve and update this particular amount since 1967, knowing the tragic results of the high inflation rate and what it has done across the country. However, while one might stand here and cast stones at the Government's inaction over the past decade or more on this matter, the point is, I suppose, that we are dealing with it today, and for that we should be thankful. I am certain that depositors across Canada will be thankful also when this legislation is finally passed.
April 12, 1983

I listened with interest when the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre was encouraging the support of the Opposition for rapid passage of this Bill when I remember instance after instance when Hon. Members of the Official Opposition, as well as Members of the New Democratic Party, were indicating their willingness to pass this Bill in a day's debate, a very limited debate. Let us get on with it now so that we can bring some sense of security, Mr. Speaker, to the people of Canada. These are such unnerving times, with uncertainty and fear across the country, that this is one small effort Parliament could make to ease the concern so many Canadians have regarding their deposits in various financial institutions. Members opposite were quite prepared to co-operate, yet when the Government House Leader said a number of days back, "We have some very important legislation on which we want the Opposition to co-operate to obtain early passage", it was interesting to note that one Bill was conspicuous by its absence from that list of Government priorities, namely Bill C-142 which would protect depositors across this country. However, let us recognize what small gains we do make these days and recognize that we are debating this legislation this afternoon and, hopefully, we will see its passage before the day is out.
While there is no question that the NDP supports this Bill in principle and will vote in favour of the principle of the Bill when we have the opportunity, we do have a number of concerns. My first concern is with regard to the amount we have identified as the insurable limit of $60,000 on a particular deposit. I recognize that you can make two cases. One, that the amount could be, and perhaps should be, higher. In the U.S. the maximum amount of coverage is $100,000, and there is no reason that we could not have that in Canada. When the Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald) presented a Private Members' Bill reflecting that upper ceiling, a number of good examples were put forward. I remember that not long afterwards I had the opportunity to raise the issue with my constituents. In speaking at a number of town hall meetings, I found people were wondering why it was necessary to have $60,000 as the maximum, let alone $100,000. Then, through discussion with a number of people there and subsequently with Members of my caucus, it became clear that when many Canadians retire they sell their home and find themselves with a sizeable piece of change. It is not unlikely to have a typical family with $60,000, $80,000 or $100,000 as a result of the sale of their home. When invested, that amount will see them through their retirement years as a supplementary income. For that reason perhaps we ought to be looking at higher levels of depositor protection. I would encourage the Minister to give this some thought in bringing forth a subsequent Bill in the months ahead to achieve the security that Canadians are seeking today.
Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, I supported the idea that it was to an investor's advantage perhaps to have his or her deposits placed in a number of institutions. We have seen the dangers in the last number of months of placing all our hopes in one particular venture, or putting all our eggs in one basket, when
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
we saw the Government's so called economic strategy consisting of the large energy megaprojects in western Canada. When those projects failed to materialize, then the hopes of that particular strategy were dashed. Again, I think we want to encourage Canadians to reflect upon the advantage of placing deposits in perhaps two, three or more institutions so that they may have better protection for those hard earned deposits. However, we still recognize that under this legislation one may have a deposit of $60,000 in one institution, $60,000 in another, and $60,000 in a shared account or shared deposit between husband and wife, which again would be protected. In the final analysis, I believe the $60,000 maximum is adequate and will serve Canadians well.
I do want to mention to the Minister that in spite of the fact he introduced this legislation for first reading back in January, 1983, and made it very clear that it was retroactive legislation, it was interesting to note that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation asked its member institutions to stop advising clients that the maximum insurance provided was $60,000. In other words, the institution was advising its clients that they do not have protection to that amount at this time. If this legislation passes the House and receives Royal Assent, then they will, but at the moment the maximum allowable insurance is $20,000. So I think Canadians were, in a sense, misled to a certain extent because Bills can be amended. At least I would hope the Government has that option open to them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Why didn't you say that about the Income Tax Act?

Perhaps the amount we are talking about is not $60,000, but it could be amended to $40,000 or $80,000 or whatever. So I believe the Minister has to be criticized for perhaps inadvertently providing a false sense of security to Canadians.
There is a particular point I want to make, Mr. Speaker, one that deserves some analysis today and which has not been discussed at length until this point, that is, whether coverage up to $60,000 is really in the best interests of the country. Leaving aside the depositor's point of view, I would ask what that does to the institution's perception of how risky a venture it is prepared to take on. When we carried out the analysis of bank profits in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, one thing became very, very evident. The banks of Canada had over-extended themselves in many areas. They had become highly exposed and consequently were considered by some to be relatively risky financial ventures. When one looks at the year-end accounts of the class "A" chartered banks of Canada, I think one has to draw the conclusion that on a number of occasions they made some very imprudent loans and found themselves in very serious and over-exposed positions, particularly when it came to sovereign loans. Perhaps this insurance protection of $60,000 will encourage those institutions, who have made imprudent loans in the past, to continue that behaviour. It is simply speculation at this point, but it is something the American Government

April 12, 1983
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
has been concerned about for some time. As a matter of fact, their deposit insurance institution has raised this issue.
I do not have to refer to the United States to remind Hon. Members that not so many years ago the Economic Council of Canada made a particular recommendation to Members of the House of Commons. I remember, when the Economic Council was before the Committee a few weeks ago, asking the President or chief executive officer of that particular group, Mr. David Slater, what he did for a living. Did he serve the people of Canada well? Did he advise the Government properly? He said that he did, and I think members of the committee felt that indeed we were receiving some relatively sound advice from the Economic Council. They were able to lay out what the problems were in terms of our economic future, and consequently the Government was expected presumably to respond favourably and positively to those recommendations. Well, back in 1976 the Economic Council of Canada recommended that deposit insurance premiums ought to reflect the specific risks involved in the same way that a bond rating company evaluates the diverse securities of Governments and corporations. This step would add to the flexibility of the system. Institutions which chose to hold safe portfolios would benefit from lower insurance premiums, whereas those holding risky portfolios would not. I want to emphasize that this is an insurance scheme, and usually insurance rates reflect the state of riskiness of a venture. If one is a driver today and has had 250 auto accidents compared to the driver who has had a safe driving record for the last 20 years, one will probably be paying a different rate. Compared to the person applying for life insurance who is 25 years old, one who is 80 years old will be paying a different rate because of the different risks. However, in this situation, regardless of what kind of risk one may be, regardless of how risky is a venture in which the financial institution is involved, one pays the same premium. That is quite a peculiar insurance company.
We have a similarly peculiar insurance company which is called the Maritime Pollution Claims Fund. That is the fund under which a certain levy is placed on every barrel of oil which comes into eastern Canada to protect the East Coast in the event of an oil spill. Whether one has a two-bit, old, beat-up, rusty ship or a super, ultra modern tanker, one pays the same rate. It is ridiculous, yet it is called an insurance fund. It is a ridiculous fund because obviously the old, tin-pot rusted out venture out there, filled with oil, is more of a risk than the ultra, super, brand-new tanker. The same is true with this piece of legislation. Certain trust companies which can go unnamed at this point because we all know what they are, which are over-extended, involving themselves in some questionable, peculiar activities which are imprudent by anyone's definition, are paying the same rate, 0.3 per cent of their insured deposits, as the venture which is the most conservative, the most laid back or, the best way to say it, the most "secure" venture available.
I guess what I am saying is that it is unfair. Not only is it unfair, but we must consider that we are in a situation which is
quite different from the one which prevailed when the Insurance Act was introduced back in 1967. At that time, when the decision was to levy a particular premium on the insured deposits of 0.3 per cent, the banking or financial system of Canada was relatively tranquil or stable. Since then, however, the situation has changed. We are in an incrediably dynamic financial situation which is changing by the month in terms of new approaches, with new technology and techniques being applied to the way in which we manage our finances. The Inspector General of Banks himself admitted that it is virtually impossible for him and his Department to keep on top of the system these days. We have a financial system out there which, to some of us at least, appears to be out of control in certain areas in terms of the people of Canada having any sense of what is going on with regard to regulations or the ability to regulate some activities.
I will use an example of some of the questionable practices of the banks in terms of their offshore ventures. I think that if the realities or the truth were ever known, if an explanation were required as to what those ventures were, which is not the case under present legislation, Canadians would be somewhat concerned. Therefore, here we are in a situation where the banks of Canada have now expanded into the international lending sphere, which is certainly much more risky in terms of the loans Canadian chartered banks make in countries such as Argentina, Mexico, Venezuela, Columbia and the like. It is questionable whether these countries will ever repay those loans. We find today that 20 per cent of 40 per cent of the total business of some of our chartered banks concerns overseas activity. Also, the total liabilities of banks have expanded to more than 30 times their shareholders' equity.
Thirty-four.

In some cases, it is as high as 34, and some months back it was as high as 38. These are highly risky, highly levered situations, again placing the situation in quite a different risk climate than we were experiencing back in 1967.
The problem that I see is that we must make some changes to the Bill before we will be happy with it. I do not believe that today is the time to offer those amendments because of the need to pass this particular legislation to bring some security to the depositors across Canada. However, I would certainly urge the Minister to consider the unfairness of requiring the same premium to be paid by both risky ventures and secure ventures. If it is really an insurance scheme, then I suggest that that ought to be changed and changed quickly.
I want to mention one other aspect which has not been considered seriously to this date. To enable the CDIC to cover deposits in the three trust companies in Ontario concerning which there was some difficulty, the federal Government must approve a loan of $500 million to the agency. The CDIC previously had only $260 million in available funds based on premiums paid to it by its 150 member institutions, including the banks and trust companies. What that means is that it was ultimately the people of Canada who had to come back and guarantee the situation. The premiums which the companies
April 12, 1983

themselves were paying, that is, .3 per cent of their insured deposits, is perhaps not adequate under these dynamic financial times to provide the necessary coverage if the CDIC had to come to the federal Government to have a $500 million loan approval offered to it. Perhaps in terms of the ultimate security to Canada's depositors, these are some of the items which should be reconsidered.

Before recognizing the Hon. Member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail), the Chair should first inquire as to whether there are questions or comments arising from the remarks of the Hon. Member who spoke last.

I would like to ask a question, Mr. Speaker. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap, who has just spoken, went on at length criticizing the operation of the
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation because, according to him, it will not operate under proper insurance principles according to which the premiums or the levy should be greater when there is greater risk. He also cited the operation of the fund which has been established to compensate people in eastern Canada who are victims of oil pollution. He said that this Bill operated the wrong way, in his opinion, because everyone was subject to the same levy. These are sound conservative insurance principles.
However, in Canada there is another insurance scheme, that is, the Unemployment Insurance scheme. This one, according to the Hon. Member's principles, presumably works backwards because the premiums are less and the benefits are greater when the risk is greater. Is the New Democratic Party advocating that unemployment insurance benefits in Newfoundland should be less than they are in Alberta, or that residents of Newfoundland should pay higher premiums? That is the natural corollary to what he was saying this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, I actually appreciate the opportunity to speak on this point because the NDP has always considered the Unemployment Insurance scheme not to be the best method of ensuring adequate incomes to people during difficult times. We have always advocated a more comprehensive universal social scheme to replace it. What the Hon. Member is making is again the kind of simplistic inquiry that one would expect from a Tory backbencher on a topic such as this. It reflects once again their, or perhaps his, inability to understand the complexity of this particular problem.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a genuine pleasure for me to participate in this debate this afternoon, to come back after our recess and sense this fresh breeze of co-operation that exists in the House this afternoon. I speak of the attitude among all Parties in the House with respect to Bill C-142, an Act to amend the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act. I certainly want to congratulate the Hon. Member who spoke before me, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), the NDP financial critic, for his positive attitude toward the importance of this Bill.
He did raise a few points in his comments about Unemployment Insurance and about the Minister's statements on this. However, I am sure he will agree, and all Canadians know, that the principle of insurance is based on sharing the risk with the largest number of people involved. It would follow, with respect to the Bill we are debating today, that the same principle would apply and the same benefits would accrue to all Canadians. The issue with which we are concerned today is a matter of bringing ourselves into the eighties and updating this measure to meet the needs of all Canadians in our modern times.

April 12, 1983
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
The main purpose of this short Bill is to increase to $60,000 the amount of protection provided by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation on savings deposits placed with financial institutions in Canada.
As most Members know, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation is a Crown corporation that was formed in the centennial year of 1967 under the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act. The main purpose of the Corporation is the insuring, within limits, of savings deposits placed by the public with member financial institutions. The existence of deposit insurance has given security and stability to the savings deposit market in Canada and has almost completely eliminated any fear of runs against financial institutions.
All banks and all federally incorporated trust companies and mortgage loan companies that accept deposits are members of the Corporation by law. Provincially incorporated trust companies and mortgage loan companies accepting deposits may become members on application if the Province of the Corporation concurs and if the financial condition of the company is acceptable to the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.
At the end of 1982, 132 federally incorporated institutions were members of the Corporation, of which 65 were banks and 67 were trust companies or loan companies. At the same time there were 52 provincially incorporated trust companies and loans companies holding membership.
At the end of 1982, the total assets of the Corporation amounted to approximately $255 million. Its income for the year amounted to approximately $14 million in the form of premiums and $25 million in the form of interest. Deposits insured by the Corporation as of April 30, 1982, amounted to $118 billion. The corporation is a tax-paying institution and is expected to pay approximately $12 million in taxes in respect of the 1982 taxation year.
The Corporation is governed by a board of directors comprising a chairman appointed by Order in Council, and, ex officio, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the Deputy Minister of Finance, the Inspector General of Banks and the Superintendent of Insurance.
The three principal purposes of the Bill are, first, to increase the maximum limit of insurance on each deposit; second, to increase the borrowing authority of the Corporation; and, third, to reduce possible misunderstanding when member institutions receive funds that are not insured deposits. In addition, there are a few technical amendments not involving any important principle.
As I indicated in my opening remarks, the Government has indicated the importance of bringing the Bill up to date to meet demands in the country today. The previous speaker referred to some recent incidents which occurred in a Province which caused great concern to many Canadians and certainly to investors and depositors.
I suggest that it speaks well of our present Government that we have accepted the responsibility of assuring Canadians that, through this Bill, they are encouraged to deposit their savings. We are showing them that we are prepared to take the
necessary action to protect them in every way possible by increasing the amount of coverage from $20,000 to $60,000.
Another attractive feature of this measure, which was referred to by the previous speaker, is the fact that this legislation is retroactive to January, 1983. The legislation is being changed in recognition of a number of changes that have taken place. Many are aware that deposit levels have risen of a consequence of inflation. The existence of deposit insurance has probably had an effect in increasing this type of savings as compared with other possibilities such as investments in bonds or stocks in the market. As well, the existence of tax deferred plans such as Registered Retirement Savings Plans and Registered Home Ownership Plans have probably also stimulated savings of the insured type. As a consequence, it seems desirable to make an increase in the level of deposit insurance at this time. The $60,000 limit proposed was recommended by the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs in its report on the profit situation of the chartered banks published last July. It is estimated that the $60,000 limit will cover approximately 78 per cent of the deposits in banks and 92 per cent of the deposits in trust companies and loan companies.
Some suggestions have been received that the limit should be set much higher than $60,000. The Government is conscious of these suggestions and also of the fact that in the United States the limit on deposit insurance under the Federal Deposit Insurance Plan has been set at $100,000. However, we believe that a limit of $60,000 would be appropriate for the Canadian plan at the present time. It is important to keep in mind that the basic purpose of the plan is to insure savings deposits rather than to insure investments at a level where the investor could be expected to exercise his own judgment or seek professional advice. It is not desirable to interfere in the normal functioning of the financial market by setting a deposit insurance guarantee at a level that puts all other types of investment activity at a disadvantage.
As well, it is important to note that the main volume of premium funds received by the corporation come from the large, strong institutions, whereas the smaller and less known institutions are probably the beneficiaries of the plans to an extent that is out of proportion to their relative size. There has to be some reasonable limit on the extent to which the large institutions are forced to contribute to a pool of this type.
The Bill proposes no change in the premium structure. Under present rules, the annual premium required of each member institution is one-thirtieth of 1 per cent of the amount of insured deposits. However, the Corporation has certain limited authority to reduce the premiums below this level if it believes that the fund is adequate.
With respect to borrowing power, the Corporation now has the power to borrow up to $500 million from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. Any such borrowing is to meet financial needs to the extent that the Corporation cannot conveniently meet these needs from its own resources. Any such loans would be at
April 12, 1983

a rate of interest that is appropriate to the circumstances and would be repaid by the Corporation, either from realization of its own assets or from the revenue produced by future premiums.
It is important, if the CDIC is to play its full role as a stabilizing influence in the savings deposit market, that it be of such size and have resources sufficient to make clear to everyone concerned that it can fulfil the function that it is intended to play. The borrowing limit of $500 million set in 1967 was adequate at the time. However, the total amount of all insured deposits is now more than six times the amount that was insured in 1967. In the context of this fact and of the increase in the insured limit from $20,000 to $60,000 it seems appropriate to provide the Corporation with access to larger financial resources to meet emergency needs. The Bill, therefore, proposes that the borrowing authority be raised from $500 million to $1.5 billion.
With respect to possible confusion where a member institution accepts money that is not insured, the Bill proposes that all member institutions be required to mark clearly any instrument issued in return for funds where the transaction does not give rise to an insured deposit. Certain exceptions are specified in the Bill where it is most unlikely that any misunderstanding would occur. The purpose of this provision is to meet certain problems that have arisen in connection with the operation of the Corporation over the years.
Because of these pertinent facts and of all the figures and other substantive information I have given, I encourage and urge Members on all sides of the House to assist us in the giving of second reading to Bill C-142 as expeditiously as possible.

Mr. Speaker, before I get into the detail of second reading debate on Bill C-142, I would like to digress a little, but no more than did the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans). He made the remark that he favoured greater federal presence in the securities business. I have some reluctance in accepting offhand that type of advice. If the federal Government gets into the business of regulating the sales and dispositions and trading in securities of corporations that are provincially chartered, I think that might cause some difficulty. If all stock exchanges in Canada were to become subject to federal regulations and all operated the same way, we might not have as good a system as we now have where legislation affecting the operation of stock exchanges is made by the various Provinces. The example that comes to mind is what happened in Ontario several years ago at the time of the MacMillan Windfall episode. At that time
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
the Ontario Securities Commission, the Ontario Stock Exchange and the Government of Ontario of that day decided they wanted to get out of the junior end of the securities business. They wanted to concentrate solely on blue chip issues such as Inco, the Bank of Montreal, Chrysler, Massey-Fergu-son and so on. When they got out of the junior end of the business, the action went to Vancouver. The Vancouver market grew and expanded because it was fulfilling a necessary function, that of raising junior capital largely for resource exploration. It was obvious to Canadians that that type of business was required in Canada. Had it been a federal decision to get out of the junior end of the business, there would have been nobody else to look to and we would probably have lost it entirely. As it is, with these things under provincial jurisdiction, people in Ontario who now realize they made a mistake want to change their rules to draw back a little of the business from Vancouver.
To get on with the second reading of Bill C-142, amendments to the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act, let me say that I, like just about every other Member of the House, am in favour of the provision to raise the maximum insurable deposit from $20,000 to $60,000. This amendment has been brought to us largely at the urging of the Opposition. We spoke out on this matter at considerable length some time ago before the crisis, the Greymac Trust and Crown Trust fiasco, which brought the matter to the attention of the Government and forced the Government to act. About the only sense of fulfillment we have on this side of the House, and presumably what will continue to happen until the time of the next election when we will then find ourselves on the other side of the House, is that once in a while we have the opportunity to say, "I told you so".
I would like to quote from Hansard of February 17, 1982 when I spoke, over a year ago on this matter under the provisions of Standing Order 43.1 said then:
Madam Speaker, in order to take into account the decrease in the value of money brought about by years of Liberal-caused inflation, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid):
That the maximum deposit insured by the Canada Deposit Insurance
Corporation be increased from the present limit of $20,000 to a more
reasonable limit of $100,000.
This allows me to say, "I told you so." It is nice to see the Government acting on my recommendations, Mr. Speaker.
What I would like to see happen in this House this afternoon is the same as what was brought to our attention by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre. We would like to see the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove), responsible for financial institutions stand in his place and give an absolute assurance that the provisions of the Bill we are debating today will apply to the victims of the Greymac Seaway disaster. There is some doubt that is the case. I see the Minister is nodding, and I hope he will do as has been asked by Members on both sides of the House today.
Personally I would have preferred it had the limit been raised to $100,000. This figure has been accepted in the
24418

April 12, 1983
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
United States of America since 1978. We are told the $60,000 limit corresponds, after taking inflation into account, to the original 320,000 set in 1967. It is pretty evident that inflation, even if controlled somewhat, will continue. The huge deficits run up by the present Government of Canada will guarantee this will happen. Therefore, it will only be a matter of a few years' time when we will have to address this issue again because the limit will have been eroded by inflation. If we now raised the limit to $ 100,000, it could probably be kept in place for a number of years.
Like the Hon. Member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail), I think that a system of deposit insurance is fundamental to a modern banking system. Any fractional reserve system of banking is inherently insolvent. On occasion the banking system, individual banks in particular, are subject to runs. The only way this can be stopped is to have the cash ready for depositors when they come to the window and ask for their money. If that cash is not available, the whole system is subject to the domino effect. One deposit-taking institution after another can fall by the wayside unless somebody has the cash handy to hand out.
Before a system of deposit insurance was brought into effect in the United States in the thirties and a little bit later in Canada, runs on banks and the collapse of banks, especially the smaller ones, were much more frequent than today. Probably one of the greatest advances made during the Depression years in order to ensure that repetitions of the disastrous financial collapses of that time would not reoccur was the institution in the United States of a federally-sponsored system of deposit insurance.
Before that was brought into effect, providing cash in times of crisis was largely up to the major bankers of the day, who sometimes rendered sterling services in making loans available to various banks and institutions that were in fear of collapse because of a run on them taking place.
It is a better system to have a federally-sponsored deposit insurance than to leave it up to the larger bankers in the country or in a particular area. Of the many Crown corporations that we have in Canada-and I do not know how many we have altogether but probably about 450 federally-in my opinion the Deposit Insurance Corporation is one that really fulfills a necessary function. It is something that Canadians can be proud of.
It is my intention to look at some of the provisions of the Bill. Of course, the most important one is the increase from
320,000	to 360,000 of insurable deposits. Everyone who has spoken on the Bill has mentioned this. There are other items in the Bill that deserve some attention.
The Hon. Member for Restigouche mentioned that the maximum amount that can be lent out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund to the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation will be increased under this Bill from the present limit of half a billion dollars to 31.5 billion. I would like to know where the 31.5 billion comes from. It is a nice round figure. I will be proposing some nice round figures later, which I would have
some difficulty in justifying absolutely. When this Bill is at Committee stage, some explanations should be given as to why the 31.5 billion is to be imposed. Why is it that figure rather than 31. billion or 32 billion? Why was it decided that the correct figure was 31.5 billion?
I agree with the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) who, when it comes to insurance is very conservative, that the Corporation should be self-financing. I agree it is necessary that the Corporation in very particular and, in unusual circumstances, should have the authority to borrow money from the Government out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. It has to have that authority for those times when everything goes awry and it needs a lot of cash at one time. Hopefully the cash can be paid back once the emergency has receded. However, by and large the operation of that Corporation should be self-financing. It should be financed out of the premiums it charges.
The present levy is one-thirtieth of 1 per cent of deposits. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap misled the House when he said that it was .3 per cent. I am sure that was inadvertent. No doubt he will have the opportunity to correct that. It was obviously just a slip of the tongue. He cited the figure wrongly by a magnitude of ten.
I understand that CDIC presently has 3260 million on hand. At least that is the figure cited in the press. It is stated that about 3200 million of this could be used up as a result of the Crown Trust default, if that is the right word. It probably is not. In any event, it is the Crown Trust case. If that were to take place, there would be virtually no cash left within the Corporation. Therefore, as a very immediate measure, it should have authority to borrow from the Government.
In my opinion, the CDIC should have a cushion of about 3500 million from which it could operate. Please do not ask me why I came up with 30.5 billion. I do not think I could explain it any better than the gentleman opposite could explain the 31.5 billion figure. It seems in the region of adequacy.
In order to build up that cushion, it might be necessary to increase the premium over the intermediate or short term. Perhaps a system could be adopted whereby the premium would be increased until the cushion was built up. I am not adverse to the insurance principles voiced this afternoon by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap, but we might have difficulty unless we have a formula based on past experience of allocating different premiums to different deposit-taking institutions. Because the premium or levy is so small a percentage, if we were to go by strict insurance principles, the levy for different institutions might not be that much. For the sake of simplicity, we might be able to live with a system of a uniform levy. After the cushion had been built up to the 3500 million range, it may be desirable to decrease the premium.
I now want to look at the different ways in which the Deposit Insurance Corporation can fulfil its function. The worst case is where an institution goes absolutely belly up, is no longer there, and the CDIC has to pay the depositors up to the maximum amount.
April 12, 1983

I am pleased to see contained within the Bill a minor amendment to Subsection 13(4) of the Act which has the effect of clearing up certain possible legal difficulties with regard to who should be paid by the Corporation. I understand that previously it had to be the depositor named in the books of the member. There might be some errors there. The owner of record of that deposit might not be the beneficial owner of that deposit, so I am pleased to see that that technical amendment has been made.
OO)
When the member deposit-taking institutions is savable, when it has not gone completely belly-up but where with a little bit of help it might get by, there are various ways in which the CDIC can operate. Formerly the main way in which it did this was to make a loan to that member. Now in the Bill there are other proposals. I am not quite certain whether CDIC had the authority to help out in these other ways, but now it is quite explicit. It now has the authority not only to make loans to the member institutions but it is to have the authority to guarantee loans. If a trust company is in difficulty and wants cash on hand to pay its depositors, it can borrow that money from a bank and CDIC now has the authority to guarantee that loan. CDIC now has the authority to make a substantial deposit in a deposit-taking institution which is in trouble, and it is pretty obvious that that has the same effect.
If depositors are standing in line wanting $200 million that probably does not exist and CDIC comes along and puts a deposit of $200 million in that institution and says that it has no intention of withdrawing those funds for some time, then the effect will be the same. It will be known that the institution has cash with which to pay its debts, make good the deposits, and the lines will discontinue.
There are certain good points about these other methods of dealing with the problem. Certainly CDIC is to be given a greater degree of flexibility than it had previously. It has a greater number of weapons in its arsenal to fight insolvency. But there are also some points about this that are not so good. First of all, when it goes into loan guarantees and deposits-making, there is no actual cash involved so it is not so hard to do and it is sometimes done under the bushel, so to speak. It is away from the eyes of the public and away from the eyes of Parliament. CDIC could perhaps over-extend itself not by cash loans but by way of loan guarantees. We see this in other areas of Government where loans have been guaranteed and the Government says, "Oh, they are never going to exercise that guarantee". But then things go from bad to worse and the Government gets hooked. I have seen that at the provincial level and it seems that I have also seen that at the federal level.
If these things are to happen, in my opinion, then there should be maximum numbers imposed on the guarantees and on the deposits in these shaky institutions and these matters should be reported regularly. These matters, I suggest, need careful study in committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Are there any Hon. Members rising to ask questions of the Hon. Member who has just spoken? If not,
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
the Chair recognizes the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke).

Mr. Speaker, I want to take just a few moments of the time of the House to add some words on Bill C-142, an Act to amend the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act. I, too, favour the principal proposal in this Bill to increase the amount of insurance on individual deposits from $20,000, which was the amount established in 1967, to $60,000, an amount that will approximately reflect the loss of purchasing power since that time.
It is worth noting that the Act covers deposits in 91 federal member institutions, including 29 banks and 62 trust and loan companies, and 54 provincial deposit-taking institutions, making the total of 145.
We have agreed, I think, that the limit of $20,000 was a ridiculously low amount and had to be changed. However, there is one principle that has not been addressed in this Bill, and that is that it was already easy under the $20,000 limit to circumvent the limit by moving funds around, by opening deposit accounts in different institutions or in different names because the $20,000 limit only applied to accounts that were held in one individual name.
Now the $60,000 will overcome the purchasing power problem but it will not change the fact that depositors will still be able to move funds around and put funds into more than one account in more than one deposit-taking institution and achieve coverage that perhaps the Government did not intend to give in this amending Bill.
I think it was another colleague, perhaps the Hon. Member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Nickerson), who suggested that there should not be any kind of limit at all. That is something that the Government-
No, it was not.

It was not the Hon. Member for the Northwest Territories. I heard another colleague suggest that we should not have any kind of limit. I think that should be studied by the Government because it is so easy to get around this $60,000 proposal by having multiple accounts in different deposit-taking institutions. Probably all our deposits should be insured. I leave that to the Government to consider.
When the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation was established in 1967, obviously it was felt that there was a need for protection for depositors. Indeed, some three years later, the Commonwealth Trust Company collapse in Vancouver confirmed that need. The loss then as recorded by the Corporation was $5 million. There was not another loss until 1980, but by then the funds had begun to build up and build up. By 1980, the Corporation had on its books a cumulative surplus of over $200 million. By the end of 1981, the surplus in the premium account was $167 million and in the accumulated earnings, $58 million; the surplus totalled $225 million at the end of 1981. I have been unable to confirm the 1982 figure but using that progression, it is now probably $260 million in surplus.

April 12, 1983
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
Where is the surplus, Mr. Speaker? A reference to the Public Accounts of Canada or the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation's annual report tells us that $82 million of that surplus is invested in Government of Canada Treasury bills and another $82 million is invested in Canada Bonds. A total of $164 million has been taken out of the CDIC and invested by the Government in its own securities.
If the money has just come out of one company and gone into the Government coffers, then I would like to know what the difference is between this kind of a levy or so-called premium and a tax. I do not think the Government will be successful in answering that question because they do not answer it about many other forms of tax like Canada Pension Plan premiums and Unemployment Insurance premiums. These things all just go into the federal pot and get lost.
If it is a tax, then is it a desirable tax? The premiums for 1980 were $22 million, and the 1981 premiums were $20 million. I suggest, and I know from the annual report, that reduced premiums have been in effect for the last ten years, presumably because the surplus is building up adequately. Well, now the surplus is building up in any event. The investment surplus in 1981 was $13 million so that to tax the companies, which amounts to taxing the depositors another $20 or $22 million, seems to be totally unnecessary. All of that money, the $20 or $22 million, could be left in the company's hands. The Bill will increase the loan capability of CDIC from $500 million to $1.5 billion. I contend that there is no need for the company to build up a surplus at the rate of $35 million or so every year. This is not a private enterprise but a Government enterprise. The Government is making it possible for the CDIC to dip into the Consolidated Revenue Fund on the basis of loans for anything from $500 million to $1.5 billion. The surplus that has been building up is totally unnecessary and leads to the kind of abuses that the Auditor General reports nearly every year.
Another reason why I say this surplus is not required is that the Department of Insurance supervises all of the deposit taking institutions and also the operations of CDIC. Banks, trust companies, mortgage and loan companies and mortgage investment companies are supervised by Government. A surplus is not necessary. Altogether, 145 companies are insured in the CDIC. Even in a year as disastrous as 1982, it is extremely unlikely that these companies would produce a substantial loss. The losses produced in any year are going to be relatively small if the experience of the last 15 years is a guide. And, of course, we should not consider 1982 as an exemplary year. If CDIC should go into a deficit position, the Government has given it the power to borrow $500 million, and is now proposing that it have the power to borrow $1.5 billion. If the borrowing power were used, it would mean lower premiums for all participants in the scheme.
Looking at the financial condition of the company and even taking into consideration what happened in 1982, it would
appear to me that the premiums could be suspended for the foreseeable future. Let the losses, if any, absorb the surplus and then, if the company needs to, let it dip into the borrowing power given under this Bill. If there is a big loss, it makes no difference if CDIC has to cash in its Government bonds-the Government then has to find the money to retire the bonds so that CDIC will have the money to pay its claimants-or, if CDIC simply goes to the Consolidated Revenue Fund and borrows $500 million or even $1.5 billion.
While we agree with speedy passage of this Bill, I appeal to the Government for a renewed assessment of the need for a surplus which is left in the hands of the Government rather than in the hands of the taxpayers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the House ready for the question?
Question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion?
Agreed.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time and, by unanimous consent, the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Francis in the Chair.
On Clause 1-

Mr. Chairman, I should like to put some questions to the Minister of State for Finance arising out of the second reading debate before we proceed to approve clauses. The Minister and I had a discussion concerning the Bill, and I think we came to an agreement but the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra has indicated that he has some concerns about the inbreeding, in effect, that is going on.
The Superintendent of Insurance is a director of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation and is responsible for the supervision and management of registered trust and mortgage companies. The Inspector General of Banks is a director and he is responsible for the banks that are covered by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. He is supposed to inspect them and look after them.
I wonder if the Minister has given any thought to changing the directorships to make sure that there is another check and balance in the process of managing the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation so that the interlocking control that seems to exist will not take place but that different people be made responsible for the Corporation than are responsible for the operation of the institutions covered by the Corporation.

Mr. Chairman, there was some discussion of the point raised by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South on the potential for change of directors or the widening of the directorships. I agree that the Superintendent of Insurance and the Inspector General of Banks are closely associated with two sectors of the economy that are large depositors in the Corporation and that this could be perceived as inbreeding.
On the other hand, I would urge that the Hon. Member consider that it is the very strength of their position that gives
April 12, 1983

them the ability to advise the Corporation. They have knowledge gained in the supervision of the industry and through that, can ensure the strength and the health of the industry. On the one hand there is a danger that they may be so close and so expert that they may overlook something. Perhaps the difficulty with an expert is that he is so good at what he does he loses the larger picture.
We have not received requests from member organizations that the directorships be changed; we have not received a submission from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs advising the Government that the membership should be changed, and we have not received submissions from the public to that effect either. I agree with the Elon. Member and we have had the thought in mind.
Because we feel that the advice has been strong and the experience in the Corporation has been good, although he might refer to a hypothetical difficulty with the directorships we are not inclined to make a change at this time. If the Hon. Member wishes to develop that line of thought further I would certainly be willing, as I am sure the directors of the Corporation would be, to consider a well presented brief. We do not see any need for the change at this time but we are willing to hear further submissions on the point.

Further to that issue, Mr. Chairman, the other directors of the Corporation are the Deputy Minister of Finance, the Governor of the Bank of Canada and one outside director. Obviously the Minister gets no complaints from the institutions. In the case of trust companies, the Superintendent of Insurance is their superintendent. You are surely not going to find them complaining about the Superintendent being their chief insurer, and you are not going to find very many banks complaining about the Inspector General of Banks. I have never heard a bank complain about that. That has been one of the concerns of the Finance Committee as to whether the banks were well enough supervised because they seem to get along in a very patsy arrangement with the Inspector General of Banks. The Deputy Minister of Finance, from the way this country is being managed right now, is probably having enough trouble just keeping the books of the country together. The Governor of the Bank of Canada tells us he has to bring on additional staff just to look after the borrowing requirements of the Government. It strikes me that the only people who are effective directors of this Corporation are the very persons who are responsible for making sure that these institutions are operating according to law.
Earlier, in the second reading debate, I brought out the fact to the Minister that we had real concerns. Indeed, I certainly expressed concern at the meetings of the Finance Committee in 1981, and subsequently with respect to how these institutions were being supervised by the Superintendent of Insurance. To have the Superintendent of Insurance, or his people, running the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation effectively really means that the Superintendent of Insurance can use the
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
Deposit Insurance Corporation to cover up his own mistakes in management. Perhaps if the Superintendent of Insurance had been on the ball and had pulled the plug on Greymac and Seaway a year ago, we would not have the problems we have today with those corporations. We certainly would not have the problem with Crown Trust because the owners of Greymac could never have purchased Crown Trust. No one would have sold it to them. They could not have financed it. Therefore, the problems that this Corporation now faces would not be there had the Superintendent of Insurance done his duty.
I ask you, therefore, could we not at this point consider that very seriously and make sure that we do not have a person who is supposed to be judge on one side and judge on the other side, policeman on one side and policeman on the other side, and no cross-reference control?

Mr. Chairman, with respect, I do not believe the Hon. Member has advanced his case. As a matter of fact, I believe he has weakened his case in his representations; the point being that he has confused the role of the Superintendent of Insurance in his relationship to the Corporation. He is merely one of the directors. Along with him, as the Hon. Member has indicated, there is the Deputy Minister of Finance, who has responsibilities to the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance has responsibilities under Acts of Parliament, the Administration Act. These Acts require the Minister and his deputy to act in accordance with law for the public good. Similarly, the obligations assumed by the Governor of the Bank of Canada are to act in the public good, not on behalf of the Superintendent of Insurance or on behalf of any other official of any other Ministry of Canada. Therefore, the role of the Superintendent of Insurance in that makeup is simply as one of the members, and he is joined by other officials who have a legislative responsibility, which is to act for the good of the public, generally. I believe there is, therefore, a safeguard built into the operation of the Corporation.
I do not want to appear quarrelsome, Mr. Chairman. I did say in my comments that the role of the Superintendent of Insurance, the former Superintendent of Insurance who has recently taken retirement, and the role of the new Superintendent of Insurance, were challenged in the courts, and at trial none of the statements which were repeated by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South were upheld by the court. I admit that that case is under appeal, but I would respectfully suggest that the Hon. Member really is jumping to conclusions when he makes those allegations. I emphatically reject the allegations made by the Hon. Member that the Superintendent of Insurance, or any officer or employee of the Government of Canada and the Department of Insurance acting for him, acted in any way which was less than the duty imposed by the statutes or any less than what a reasonable and efficient officer of the Government would have been required to do under their circumstances of employment. That is the case which the Government put in the Federal Court of Canada. It was one, as I have indicated, which was upheld by the independent judiciary. I certainly hope that the Hon. Member is not casting

April 12, 1983
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
any aspersions on the judiciary in his wide brush condemnation of staff, because it is not supported by the judiciary.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the Minister, in light of the fact that Crown Trust, Greymac and Seaway are all provincial institutions, whether he could clarify to me what the role of the federal Superintendent of Insurance is with regard to the regulations of provincially chartered institutions?

Mr. Chairman, I thank the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre for that question. It gives me the opportunity of indicating that, of course, in the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec it is the provincial ministries which are responsible for the licensing and supervision of provincially-incorporated companies, and that includes Crown Trust, Seaway Trust and Greymac Trust. Giving the Hon. Member for Mississauga South the benefit of the doubt, I thought, when he used simply the name of Greymac and Seaway, that conceivably he may have been referring to Seaway Mortgage and Greymac Mortgage, which are, of course, federally incorporated companies. The Hon. Member will know that he raised these very questions at the Finance Committee meeting. He asked the Superintendent what circumstances prevailed vis-a-vis these companies during the last few months. The Superintendent responded that they have been on short licence and that the Superintendent had been monitoring their performance very closely, and was monitoring them very closely up until the month of December, 1982. The Superintendent was not satisfied with the performance of the companies, notwithstanding the warnings and requests that they comply with the statutes. They moved in the first week in January to assume control under Section 73 of the Act.

Mr. Chairman, that is most interesting but I thought we were talking about the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. I was wondering if the Minister could tell me, if the directors of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation are not responsible for enforcing the Act, who is? Are the Seaway Trust Company, the Crown Trust Company and the Greymac Trust Company not insured under the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation? And does the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation not provide, under Section 24 and Section 25, that if that Corporation is not satisfied the securities are available to satisfy the requirements of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, it is required to do something to effect the closing down of those companies and prevent those companies from taking deposits insured under the provisions of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act? Does that not mean that he is also responsible as the Minister designated in the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation?

Mr. Chairman, this is really a rehash of the questions we went over in this morning's deliberation. At that time I pointed out that by way of agreement between the Province of Ontario and the federal Government, the Province
has the responsibility for supervision and inspection of provincially incorporated companies. Reports are made available to the Superintendent of Insurance as the agent for CDIC federally. But it is not as if the Department is acting in isolation. I have indicated in the House and Committee that, because the Superintendent was already involved with subsidiary companies of Seaway, Greymac and Crown, both the federal and provincial ministries had taken parallel steps to indicate their concern and moved to exercise supervisory control over those companies. So that although the major responsibility is with the Province, the federal Department was aware of difficulties and had moved in areas in which it has specific responsibility to take specific steps to protect depositors as well as the interests of the Corporation.

Mr. Chairman, I have two questions for the Minister. In his speech he set out the number of financial institutions covered by the statute. Are there a number of financial institutions not presently covered, and which ones are they so that Canadians can be aware of that?
My officials advise that there are none that we are aware of, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, the Government has chosen to limit the amount to $60,000. We of course would like to see it at $100,000 because first, that coincides with the United States whith which we have a lot of investment going back and forth and we might as well synchronize with them, and, second and more important, some innocent people will be caught even with a $60,000 amount if there were ever a major catastrophe. That compares to the more sophisticated investor who will put his money into more than one institution and cover himself for 100 per cent. Why are we leaving at risk the less sophisticated person with, say, $100,000 who puts it in just one bank account?

Mr. Chairman, in my opening remarks I attempted to explain that when the Act was originally introduced it was designed to protect the ordinary investor in Canada. It was not designed to provide total protection to everyone, certainly not, for example, to those large companies or very wealthy individuals who would have the advantage of lawyers or accountants to advise them in their investment practices. By and large the result of the move to $60,000 would bring a great measure of protection to the majority of Canadians. As I recall the figures, it was something like 92 per cent of deposits in trust companies and somewhere in the high seventies for banks.
I would remind the Hon. Member of the study done by the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and Members on both sides of the House, who looked into this issue in detail. The basis of their recommendation to increase the maximum amount from $20,000 to $60,000 had to do with the general performance of the economy. I would also remind him that if he is using the American experience as a precedent, then he should be aware that there is a move afoot in the United States to decrease the $100,000 maximum because the experience is that it is too rich. The American administration
April 12, 1983

in certain areas has now moved to actually limit the $100,000 and to reduce it in certain categories. So I think that for those reasons the $60,000 is an adequate amount.

Mr. Speaker, would the Minister confirm that the exposure to the Consolidated Revenue Fund is $118 billion? If there was a total collapse, that presumably would be the amount to be paid out less the value of the bank's assets which could be recovered. Could the Minister tell us what the value of those banks would likely be and what the exposure to the Consolidated Revenue Fund would be?
Those facts are correct, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, when the sum of $60,000 was determined, was the rationale simply the increase in inflation since 1967, and did it also include consideration given to the changing nature of the financial institutions in Canada since 1967 and their over-all exposure?

Mr. Chairman, I was not a member of the committee which studied bank profits and made the recommendations, but I have read it. I think both those matters were taken into account by committee members. As I recall, the most important one, and one on which they spent some time in demonstrating mathematical parallels, was the one having to do with inflation. In other words, you will find that 60 per cent is very close to the actual inflationary experience in the economy from 1967 to the time the committee considered the matter.

Mr. Chairman, I would like some clarification regarding the fees paid on the insured deposit. Do all participating members, regardless of whether they have participated since 1967 or perhaps others who have been participating since 1977, do they all pay .03 per cent of their insurable deposits on an annual basis, or is there some differentiation depending on the length of time a firm has been participating?
Mr. Chairman, the answer is yes. It is a uniform amount irrespective of time involved.

Mr. Chairman, I would like clarification of Clause 8(2), which says that in order to be eligible for deposit insurance a deposit must be repayable on or before the expiration of five years. I would like an explanation of that, and I would also like to know whether there are going to be other considerations set out in regulations concerning the payment of $60,000 or any portion thereof?

Mr. Chairman, as to the second part of the question, no, there are no more regulations affecting additional requirements. Secondly, the five-year deposit has always been the practice of the Corporation. This merely clarifies the practice. The thinking behind the Clause is that again the Corporation and the legislation were not designed to insure long-time deposits. It was for the average Canadian depositor, and experience shows that the majority of people in ordinary
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
circumstances would not be investing beyond that period. It was a judgment call.

Mr. Deputy Speaker, my second question is, when is the Bill to come into force? I notice that Clause 9
states:
Subsections 3(1) and (2) shall be deemed to have come into force on January 17, 1983.
Subclause (2) states that Sections 4 and 7 shall come into force upon proclamation. I wonder why the entire Act is not coming into force upon Royal Assent. Is there some reason for delaying the bringing of this Section into force or into effect?

Mr. Chairman, Clause 9(1), which makes reference to Subsections 3(1) and (2), deals with a part of the Act addressing the amounts, the change from $20,000 to $60,000. The setting of the day upon which it was to come into effect was to ensure that it came into effect as soon as possible. After all, the whole objective is to bring that kind of peace of mind and security to ordinary Canadian depositors as quickly as possible.
On that point, the Member for Mississauga South and I have had discussions on a possible change in the date so as to secure peace of mind for a number of people involved in present difficulties with some companies in the Province of Ontario.
The other part dealing with Sections 4 and 7 concerns the question of stamping and the way in which depositors are made aware as to whether a deposit is covered by the Act. It is felt that the institutions will need some time in order to amend their business practices and put that into place. Therefore, it was thought that there should be some flexibility to ensure that all member companies in the Corporation have sufficient time to allow them to be ready to administer it properly. That is the only reason some flexibility was retained.

I would like to ask one short question. Just to make it abundantly clear, does the balance of the Act, other than those Sections, come into effect upon Royal Assent? Second, I understood from what the Minister said that there is likely to be an amendment to Clause 9(1) later today.
