subtopic: REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT-HAWKER SIDDELEY PLANT AT TRENTON, N.S.-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE
REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT-HAWKER SIDDELEY PLANT AT TRENTON, N.S.-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I once more raised the issue of Government orders for the Hawker Siddeley railcar plant at Trenton, Nova Scotia. I was assured at that time by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lumley) that he was concerned about the plant and the work force which has been idle for so long. We were also informed that the Minister has in the past tried to expedite orders for Nigeria, that he met with the Chief Executive Officer of the plant and also expressed the hope that this company would be able to take advantage of developments in offshore oil exploration. I personally, and 1 am sure most people in my riding appreciate these sentiments of the Minister. We appreciate his good intentions, but the path to hell is often paved with good intentions.
I am here today to raise the issue once more with the Minister and to point out that by comparison not very much is

April 12, 1983
Adjournment Debate
being done to find relief for this key industry in a town in Nova Scotia that is almost entirely dependent upon it. I do not want to be unreasonable, Sir, or unrealistic in calling upon the Government to expedite orders for this industry. I only want the Government to do in a small way what it has been doing for other large employers in other areas of the country at much greater cost.
We need and can use, if we are to believe the government's own policy statements, additional railway rolling stock. We need the jobs desperately in this part of Canada from where I come. We do not, for example, really need Challenger jets to develop our country, particularly the ones that are showing such unreliability and are being produced at such terrible cost by a company that everyone knows is being subsidized by a tremendous amount of frontend debt guaranteed by this Government, an amount probably well in excess of $1 billion. If we are talking about value for money or reasonable job creation, certainly we will not find it in the way Canadair is being managed or operated.
To use another comparison, CN Marine, another example of profligate spending, probably spent between $80 million and $90 million constructing a new CN ferry to operate between Borden, P.E.I. and Tormentine, New Brusnwick. The new vessell, the Abegweit, is the closest thing I have seen lately to the sea going equivalent of a car that is popularly known as a lemon. It is a vessel that has not been performing satisfactorily. The sad part of it is that the former vessel which had performed for many years could have been renovated and would have served well for another decade if $3 million or $4 million had been spent upgrading it, the same amount of money that was probably earned, in interest by CN Marine when in my opinion it squirrelled away $25 million, meant to pay for the new vessel, and kept it in an unauthorized bank account for many months.
I make these comparisons, Sir, to support my plea to the Government opposite to use a little bit of selectivity and common sense when it is dealing with large amounts of taxpayers money.
Instead of having a good vessel, perfectly serviceable, which would have freed $70 million or $80 million for useful purposes, we sold this vessel to a Chicago yacht club for considerably less than $100,000 Canadian dollars, a travesty if I ever saw one. Contrast that kind of economic stupidity with the real economic benefit that could accrue if some large orders for railcars in this amount were placed with this key industry in this town in Nova Scotia; an industry, I emphasize, that has a work force of nearly 2,000 people when the plant is employed at full capacity. There would be very little net cost to the Government in doing this because this work force, through no fault of its own, is drawing unemployment insurance benefits when it could be producing something useful.
People in my area are getting very tired of the inequalities and inequities of seeing money thrown around in certain constituencies in this country where jobs are maintained or created, regardless of the expense. Yet there is no money to
ensure work by producing useful commodities or useful machinery; something that would be far more appropriate than many of the profligate schemes that are being used to buy types of equipment and vessels, such as the one I mentioned, purchases that could easily be deferred for many years.
It is very little wonder that people in this country have lost faith in the judgment and capacity of Ministers of the Crown when day after day in the House of Commons we hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) say that our economy is performing satisfactorily at a time when we have record unemployment and record budgetary deficits. Most Canadians see the difference clearly between the way things are and the way they could be if a little more attention was paid to practical, sound, businesslike and appropriation practices in Government, with less attention paid to party politics and favouritism in subsidizing some industries and not others.
Instead of getting the taxpayers heavily involved with companies like Canadair, de Havilland, Massey-Ferguson, Maislin, to name just a few, it would be nice to see the Government stretch a point and make sure that certain useful equipment and machinery was ordered from companies that have not had to go to the public trough, but are still capable of producing it. These types of ventures would pay off. When they were completed, if the economy is as rosy as the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister seem to think it is going to be, and that we are in the midst of a recovery, which we all hope is and will be the case, we would have value for our money. There would be something there to justify these expenditures.
At the present time we are getting very tired of seeing selective largess in certain areas of the country at the taxpayers' expense, when in many instances there are good corporations that are capable of producing useful work, if only the Government would use a little common sense and expedite these kinds of orders.

subtopic: MEDICAL CARE-STATUS OF PROPOSED CANADA HEALTH ACT DRAFTING OF LEGISLATION
MEDICAL CARE-STATUS OF PROPOSED CANADA HEALTH ACT DRAFTING OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 17, I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) to tell the House what sort of timeframe she had in mind for the tabling of the proposed new Canada health act and encouraged her to put an actual proposal before the Canadian people so that there could be informed and concrete debate about what she has in mind for the founding principles of medicare and for the future of medicare itself. The Minister said then that the Department of Justice was drafting a document, but that it was important to take the time needed to get a better act than what we have now.
On March 29, I asked her to speed up the process by which Canadians would get the long-awaited Canada Health Act, and get it in a form that would prevent what has happened the previous day when Alberta announced that it was imposing, as
Adjournment Debate
of October 1 of this year, a variety of user fees for emergency, out-patient and in-patient services, on top of the recent hikes in premiums in that Province and the toleration of a 35.5 per cent extra billing rate.
The Minister replied that I was being too future-minded and not cognizant enough of the powers she now has under existing legislation to do something about what is going on in Alberta.
My point, however, is this. All that the Minister can do under the existing legislation is withdraw all, and I repeat, all federal health payments from Alberta. This is clearly an option that is drastic in nature and which involves both known and unknown risks to our national health care system. It was an option which was rejected by the Special Parliamentary Task Force on Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements, which recommended instead that some more gradual form of penalty be designed for Provinces perceived to be violating the principles of medicare. Existing legislation simply does not provide the federal Government with the kind of flexibility and mano-euvering room it needs, forms of which it gave up in 1977 against NDP advice to the contrary.
This is why the Minister must now make clear her proposals for a new Canada health act and how those proposals address, among other things, the need for ways to enable the federal Government to enforce and encourage practices which respect the five founding principles of medicare. The Minister must do more than wait for public opinion to work, as she did in New Brunswick. New Brunswick is not a one-Party state like Alberta, and, in any case, it is about time that this Minister actually did something about the erosion of medicare, instead of just talking about it. I suggest to her that tabling a proposal for debate, around which, hopefully, all pro-medicare people could rally, is what she must do as soon as is humanly possible.
While she is at it, she might also try to put back some of the money that was withdrawn from EPF payments just about a year ago, a step which clearly eroded her bargaining power with the Provinces and which has provided a cover for those in Alberta, Ontario and B.C., who for philosophical reasons have always resented medicare and who see in federal reductions and in the recession in general an opportunity to advocate their idealogical preferences under the guise of economic realism, instead of coming out and saying honestly to the Canadian public that they prefer more privatization of medicare.
I realize many of the difficulties involved if the Minister were to bring forward an Act without getting prior agreement from the Provinces, but I think it is at the point where she needs to act. She needs to put clear and supportable proposals before this House and before the Canadian people so that all pro-medicare people can rally to the cause of a new Canada health act which will prevent the kinds of things we are seeing happening to medicare at the hands of Progressive Conservative provincial Governments in this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Schroder (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: MEDICAL CARE-STATUS OF PROPOSED CANADA HEALTH ACT DRAFTING OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, regarding the current status of the Canada health act, the Minister of

April 12, 1983
Adjournment Debate
National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) would like to strongly assure all Canadians that the development of a new Act is proceeding as quickly as is possible, given the importance of this issue.
The Provinces and others have consistently requested that the Minister put before them, in black and white, just how she intends to strengthen our existing health insurance program and specifically how she proposes to encourage the elimination of extra billing and user charges. This is exactly what she intends to do in the very near future. The Minister believes it is essential that this extremely valuable program not be allowed to deteriorate to the point where many Canadians feel they cannot get the health care they need because of various barriers that have grown in the program.
The current Canadian Medical Association campaign against the Canada health act represents the view of only a small number of the physician population of Canada which has been attempting unsuccessfully to generate general public fears about Government involvement in assuring health services to all Canadians. It has however been repeatedly made clear to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that Canadians want prepaid universal health insurance, without barriers to necessary services. She is committed to preserving this Canadian privilege.
Other professional and public groups have made known to the Minister that they would like to see insured health services shift toward health prevention and promotion. Much as she supports these moves, and the support of the federal Government is evident in grants to the provinces for extended health care services, our present system of insured health care services has a long and strong tradition and is, therefore, slow to change. While such changes evolve in our health care services, the role of the federal Government must be to facilitate such moves, but at the same time not lose the insured health services that Canadians can depend on now. Public interest in health and health care has never been higher, and we all recognize that health care services will have to be increasingly responsive to the expectations of the public. The Minister of National Health and Welfare will not fail to do her part in strengthening our national insured health service program through the introduction of new health legislation, following a meeting which she expects to have with her provincial colleagues.

Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley) to recall the failure of the bilateral negotiations for quotas on imports of clothing and textiles from South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and China. I asked him to confirm that imports are up by 18.8 per cent this year compared to last year, and to tell us when Cabinet will decide to impose unilateral quotas as requested by the industry.
The Minister was party to those negotiations and meetings but he ducked the question. I understand why he chose not to answer. It is because the Cabinet does not want to make up its mind. I also understand why he passed the question to the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan)- because that Minister was not in the House to be asked. Nevertheless, the industry wants this question answered. Will the Government protect the 150,000 workers directly employed in this industry from unfair competition?
The fact is that according to the Government's own reports, mainly the Textile and Clothing Board reports of 1980, 1981 and 1982, the textile and clothing industry of Canada is competitive; it is efficient; it is technically on a par with the industries of other countries. The productivity of this industry is as good as the productivity of other manufacturing industries in Canada, or is better than average. The capital investment rate in this industry is larger than the capital investment rate in most secondary manufacturing in Canada. In other words, we are not suffering from fair competition. We are not suffering from competition simply in terms of putting out good work and being productive.
The competition we are suffering is the result of excessively low wages, about 49 cents per hour in the Philippines in 1979, or $1.27 an hour in South Korea a year ago. These low-wage countries have been increasing their exports of clothing into Canada in the last two or three years. Yet Canada absorbs only about 1 or 2 or 3 per cent of the production of countries such as South Korea, Brazil, the Philippines, Singapore and Hong Kong. Far more could come in from those countries which have wages that no one in this House would ask Canadians to accept. No Member opposite would dare ask his constituents to work for 50 cents an hour and support a family on that. Yet, this is the implication of the Government's policy.
The Government argues that if imports are restricted, clothing prices will rise too quickly. Yet it is the price of the import which has been rising at a faster rate than the cost of living and it is the price of Canadian made clothing which has been rising at a slower rate than the cost of living. In other words, if Canadian competition is taken out of that industry, the import prices will rise much faster yet, and the consumers of Canada will be the losers.
There is no gain to Canada in destroying an industry which employs 150,000 people, mostly women, many of whom are the sole supporters of their families. There is no gain to Canada in destroying an industry which indirectly employs another
100,000	in terms of supplying material and services. There is no gain to Canada in losing the buying power of 250,000 more workers, adding them to the two million people who are already out of work.
It is the duty, therefore, of this Government to defend the garment and textile industry of Canada against unfair competition, competition based on excessively low wages. It is the duty of the Government to protect our workers against unfair competition because there is no benefit in forcing Canadians to
April 12, 1983

work for 50 cents an hour. There is no benefit in destroying the industry which provides the bulk of the clothing of Canadians. Canadians, with our severe climate, would then become absolutely dependent on clothing imported from foreign companies under the control of large multinational companies which would then be able to force prices up.
If the Government wishes to force wages down by promoting unemployment, and by destroying established industries of Canada, then the policy it is following is quite logical. This Government will have to answer for its actions, if two million unemployed become three million unemployed next year because of its policy of promoting unfair wage competition.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Maltais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased to hear what the Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) had to say. I think the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is extremely sensitive to the concerns that were expressed by the Hon. Member with respect to import quotas for clothing, in the same way the Department was last year on the subject of import quotas for shoes. In the latter case, the Government achieved very good results by revising quotas and thus giving Canadians an opportunity to manufacture products for Canadian consumers.
As far as the clothing negotiations are concerned, the Hon. Member knows perfectly well that these involve bilateral agreements and, in fact, the entire spectrum of international trade. When the agreements are signed, we will have a certain number of responsibilities and if there were any changes, there might be penalties for countries that break the agreement once it is signed. Nevertheless, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley) already announced six months ago,
Adjournment Debate
in October 1982, a number of short-term measures leading up to negotiations with Korea, Hong Kong and China on certain changes that would make the import quota system more flexible. These negotiations have been more or less satisfactory, but there is still a lot of work to be done. Cabinet intends to make a statement on a clothing import policy as soon as the policy has been revised. This is being done at the present time, and it is one of our top priorities, because the Government is indeed very sensitive to the concerns expressed by the Hon. Member, and we certainly do not want anyone in Canada to be adversely affected by any import policy. On the contrary, it has never been the intention of this Government to make Canadian workers work for 50 cents an hour.
However, the Hon. Member will understand the Government's position with respect to its commitments to other countries. There is a matter of trust involved among various partners, because there are many different agreements covering clothing, cars, certain kinds of ores exchanged between countries, and so on. If countries were to unilaterally change contracts that were entered into on a voluntary basis in a perfectly normal way, one could hardly expect a climate of trust to exist. Therefore, before taking any radical unilateral measures, the Government prefers to explore all possible avenues, and I think that, not necessarily very soon but in the near future at least, the Government intends to act responsibly and make a very clear statement to the Canadian people on what it intends to do with respect to import quotas on clothing.
